So normal urine contains water, urea, extra salts and creatinine, a waste made by muscles. Blood in urine is a sign something is wrong, such as an infection or a kidney stone, and should be checked by a doctor.

notes: Kidneys saving water: sign of dehydration
Can happen when fluid is low
reason: Pale urine means you have enough water; the others are signs of dehydration.
explain: When you lose more water than you drink, your kidneys hold back water and make a small amount of dark, concentrated urine. You may also get a dry mouth, headache or dizziness. Pale straw-coloured urine shows the kidneys have enough water to work with.

notes: Very little water, lots of salt
reason: Salty chips add almost no water and make you thirsty; the others help you stay hydrated.
explain: You get water from drinks and from watery foods like fruit and soup. Salty, dry snacks give almost no water, and the extra salt makes your body need more water to flush it out through the kidneys. That is why salty food makes you thirsty.

notes: Knot of capillaries where filtering starts
Tiny air sac in the lungs
Cup that catches the filtered liquid
Twisting tube that takes back useful things
reason: An alveolus is an air sac in the lungs; the others are parts of a nephron.
explain: A nephron is a tiny filtering unit in the kidney. Blood is filtered in the glomerulus, and the liquid is caught by Bowman's capsule. As it flows along the tubule, useful things like glucose, salts and most water are taken back into the blood. What is left drains into a collecting duct as urine.

reason: The gall bladder is a digestive organ; the rest are part of the lymphatic system.
explain: The lymphatic system is a network of thin vessels and small organs. It drains extra fluid from your tissues and returns it to the blood, filtering it on the way. Lymph nodes, tonsils, the spleen and the thymus all hold white blood cells that fight germs. The gall bladder stores bile and belongs to the digestive system.

reason: Making bile is a liver job; the others are kidney jobs.
explain: Kidneys do more than make urine. By deciding how much water and salt to let go, they keep the amount of water and the salt level in your blood steady. If you drink a lot, they make more urine; if you are low on water, they make less. Bile is made by the liver to help digest fat.

items: Recycles iron from old red cells
notes: Liver job: makes a poison safer
Liver job: clears chemicals from blood
Liver job: saves iron for new cells
Liver job: some waste leaves in poop
reason: Storing urine is the bladder's job; the others are cleaning jobs of the liver.
explain: The liver is the body's chemical cleaning plant. It changes ammonia, a poisonous waste from protein, into urea, which the kidneys remove. It breaks down medicines and other chemicals, recycles iron from worn-out red blood cells, and sends some wastes out in bile, which leaves the body with poop. Urine is stored in the bladder.

notes: Water vapour lost in each breath
Makes you sweat and lose water
reason: Drinking juice adds water; the others make the body lose water.
explain: Your body loses water in several ways: urine, sweat, breath and a little in poop. Hot weather and exercise raise sweat losses a lot. To stay balanced, you need to take in as much as you lose, mostly from drinks and watery foods.

notes: Filters old cells and germs from blood
reason: The heart pumps but does not filter; the others act as filters.
explain: Your body has several filters. Kidneys filter waste from blood, lymph nodes trap germs from lymph, the spleen removes worn-out red blood cells and germs from blood, and tonsils catch germs entering the throat. The heart is a pump that moves blood to all these places; it does not filter anything.

notes: Keeps you out of direct sun
Lets sweat dry and heat escape
reason: A thick jacket traps heat; the others help the body stay cool on a hot day.
explain: Your body keeps its inside temperature close to 37 °C. On hot days, sweat glands release sweat, and as it evaporates it carries heat away from your skin. You can help by resting in shade, wearing loose light clothes and drinking water to replace what you sweat out.

notes: Thin tube that carries urine onward
Holds food for a few hours
reason: The ureter only carries urine; the others are stretchy stores that hold something for a while.
explain: Some organs act as storage bags so your body can release things at the right time. The bladder holds urine, the gall bladder holds bile until a meal arrives, the stomach holds food while it churns, and the rectum holds poop. The ureter is a thin tube that moves urine from the kidney to the bladder; it does not store it.

notes: Less salt for kidneys to remove
reason: A plaster cast treats broken bones; the others are care for kidney failure.
explain: When kidneys fail, waste and water build up in the blood. Dialysis uses a machine and filter to clean the blood instead. A kidney transplant gives the patient a working kidney from a donor. Eating less salt and controlling how much fluid they drink reduces the load while the kidneys cannot do their job.

notes: Lymph job: returns fluid to blood
Lymph job: special vessels in villi
Heart job; lymph has no pump
reason: Pumping blood is the heart's job; the others are jobs of the lymphatic system.
explain: Some liquid leaks out of tiny blood vessels and bathes your cells. The lymphatic system collects this extra fluid, filters it through lymph nodes, and returns it to the blood. It also carries digested fats from the intestine and holds many white blood cells. Lymph has no heart; body movements squeeze it along.

items: Make a hormone for red blood cells
Keep blood from getting too acidic
notes: Kidney job: tells bone marrow to make more
Kidney job: helps bones get calcium
Kidney job: adjusts salt and water
reason: Insulin comes from the pancreas; the other four are extra jobs of the kidneys.
explain: Besides making urine, kidneys have other jobs. They release a hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells, turn vitamin D into its active form, help control blood pressure, and remove extra acid. This is why people with failing kidneys can become anaemic and have weak bones. Insulin is made by the pancreas.

items: About the size of a fist
Near the back, below the ribs
In the chest beside the heart
answer: In the chest beside the heart
notes: True: curved like a kidney bean
True: one on each side of the spine
True: partly protected by lower ribs
False: kidneys are in the back of the belly
reason: Kidneys are not in the chest; the other four statements about kidneys are true.
explain: Most people have two kidneys, each shaped like a bean and roughly the size of a fist. They sit at the back of the belly, one on each side of the spine, partly protected by the lowest ribs. The heart and lungs are higher up, in the chest.
fact: The right kidney usually sits a little lower than the left, because the liver is above it.

clues: Most people have two, one on each side of the spine, just below the ribs at the back.
Each one contains about a million tiny cleaning units called nephrons.
These organs take waste and extra water out of what the heart pumps, making the yellow liquid you flush away.
explain: Kidneys are your body's main cleaners. All your blood passes through them many times a day. They filter out urea, extra salts and extra water to make urine, while keeping useful things like glucose and blood cells in the blood.
fact: Your kidneys filter about 180 litres of liquid from your blood each day, but return almost all of it, leaving about 1.5 litres of urine.

clues: In an adult it can hold about half a litre.
Its stretchy muscle wall sends signals to your brain as it fills up.
Two thin tubes bring liquid waste into this bag from the kidneys.
explain: The bladder is a stretchy, muscular bag low in your belly. It collects urine from the kidneys so you do not have to go all the time. As it fills, nerves tell your brain, and you feel the urge to go. A ring of muscle stays tight until you decide to release it.

clues: About 95 out of every 100 parts of it are water.
It carries urea and extra salts out of the body.
It gets darker and stronger-smelling when you have not drunk enough.
explain: Urine is the liquid waste made by your kidneys. It is mostly water, with urea, salts and other wastes dissolved in it. Its colour is a quick guide: pale straw means you are well hydrated, while dark yellow means you need to drink more.

clues: Long play in hot sun, vomiting or diarrhoea can cause it.
Signs include headache, tiredness and dark urine.
It happens when the body loses more fluid than it takes in.
explain: About 60% of your body weight is water, and every cell needs it. When you lose more fluid than you take in, through sweat, vomiting or diarrhoea, you become dehydrated. Your kidneys respond by making less, darker urine. Drinking water, or ORS after vomiting or diarrhoea, puts the fluid back.

clues: A part of your brain notices when your blood becomes too salty.
It is your body's alarm that fluid is running low.
Your mouth feels sticky and you really want a glass of something.
explain: Thirst is a feeling your brain creates when your blood gets too concentrated, meaning too much salt for the amount of water. At the same time, the brain signals the kidneys to save water. Both help bring your water level back to normal. In hot weather, drink before you feel very thirsty.

clues: Not drinking enough fluid for a long time raises the chance of getting one.
Minerals in liquid waste clump together into a hard lump.
When it moves down the tube towards the bladder it causes very bad cramps in the side and back.
explain: When urine is very concentrated, minerals in it can form crystals that grow into hard lumps called kidney stones. Small ones may pass out on their own; as they squeeze down the thin ureter they can cause severe pain. Drinking enough water keeps urine dilute and lowers the chance of stones forming.

clues: You have two of these, each about 25 to 30 centimetres long in an adult.
Muscles in their walls squeeze liquid waste downward in small spurts.
Each one links a bean-shaped cleaning organ to the storage bag in your lower belly.
explain: Each kidney has one ureter, a narrow muscular tube that carries urine down to the bladder. Its walls squeeze in waves, so urine moves even when you are lying down. Do not confuse it with the urethra: there are two ureters but only one urethra, which carries urine out of the body.

clues: You have only one of these, and it is much shorter in girls than in boys.
A ring of muscle around its start lets you choose when to go to the toilet.
It is the last passage liquid waste travels through before it leaves the body.
explain: The urethra is the tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body. Muscles around it stay closed until you choose to go. Because it is shorter in girls, germs can reach the bladder more easily, which is why girls get bladder infections more often and should wipe from front to back.

clues: Each one has a cup-shaped end wrapped around a knot of tiny blood vessels.
A long, twisting tube follows, where useful things are taken back into the blood.
Each of your two bean-shaped cleaning organs is packed with these tiny working parts.
explain: A nephron is the kidney's tiny filtering unit, and each kidney has about a million of them. Blood is filtered at one end, then the liquid flows along a twisting tubule. On the way, useful things such as glucose, salts and most of the water are taken back into the blood. What remains becomes urine.

clues: It is made when the body breaks down extra amino acids.
It is made from ammonia, which is poisonous, so the body changes it into this safer substance.
Your kidneys remove it from the blood, and a little leaves in sweat too.
explain: When your body uses protein, it produces ammonia, which is poisonous. The liver quickly turns ammonia into urea, which is much less harmful. Urea travels in the blood to the kidneys, which remove it in urine. It is the main waste in urine after water.

clues: Many patients need this about three times a week, for around four hours each time.
Their own filtering organs have failed, so this treatment does the job instead.
A tube carries the patient's red body fluid through an artificial filter and back again.
explain: Dialysis is a treatment for people whose kidneys have stopped working. Their blood is pumped through a machine with a special filter that removes waste and extra water, then returned to the body. It keeps the patient healthy but does not cure the kidneys, so many patients wait for a kidney transplant.

clues: No heart pumps this; your muscles squeeze it along when you move.
It travels in its own set of thin vessels, separate from arteries and veins.
It drains back into the blood after passing through small bean-shaped stations that trap invaders.
explain: Some of the liquid part of blood leaks out of capillaries to bathe your cells. Most goes back, but the extra is collected by lymph vessels and is then called lymph. It passes through lymph nodes, where white blood cells catch germs, and then rejoins the blood near the heart.

clues: Breathing out carbon dioxide is one example of it.
Sweating out salts and urea is another example.
It is the name for getting rid of harmful leftovers made by your own cells.
explain: Your cells make waste as they work, such as carbon dioxide and urea. Excretion is the removal of these wastes from the body. Kidneys, lungs, skin and liver all take part. Getting rid of undigested food as poop is usually called egestion, because that food was never part of your cells.

clues: Blood pressure here is high, which pushes water and small molecules out.
It sits inside a cup called Bowman's capsule.
It is a tiny knot of thin blood vessels where cleaning the blood begins in each kidney unit.
explain: The glomerulus is a tight knot of tiny blood vessels at the start of each nephron. Blood enters under high pressure, so water, salts, glucose and urea are squeezed out into Bowman's capsule. Blood cells and large proteins are too big to pass and stay in the blood.

clues: Fish release it straight into the water around them.
It forms when the body breaks down amino acids from extra protein.
This harmful chemical is quickly changed into a safer substance so the kidneys can remove it.
explain: Protein contains nitrogen. When the body breaks down extra amino acids, the nitrogen ends up in ammonia, which is poisonous even in small amounts. Fish can release it directly into the water. Humans cannot, so the liver turns it into urea, which is safer to carry in the blood until the kidneys remove it.

clues: Each minute, about one-fifth of everything your main pump sends out flows through this pair.
Each one branches straight off the aorta, the body's largest main pipe.
It carries waste-filled supply into the bean-shaped cleaning organs.
explain: 'Renal' means to do with the kidneys. Each renal artery carries blood from the aorta into a kidney to be cleaned. The kidneys get about a fifth of the blood the heart pumps, far more than their size suggests, because cleaning blood is their job. Cleaned blood leaves through the renal vein.

clues: Your body's movers make it at a steady rate every day as they use energy.
Doctors measure its level in a sample from a vein to check how well the filtering organs work.
If the filtering organs slow down, this substance builds up instead of leaving in urine.
explain: Creatinine is a waste made by muscles at a fairly steady rate. Healthy kidneys remove it from the blood into urine. Because its production is steady, a high creatinine level in a blood test is a sign the kidneys are not filtering well, and doctors use it to check kidney health.

scenario: Arjun played football for two hours in the afternoon sun and drank almost nothing. Now he has a headache, a dry mouth and dark yellow urine. What is the most likely problem?
optionNotes: Causes sharp pain in side or back
Lost more water than he drank
Reaction to a food, often with rash
Would follow an injury, with swelling
explain: Playing in the heat makes you sweat a lot. If you do not drink, your body runs low on water. The kidneys save water by making a small amount of dark urine, and a dry mouth and headache follow. Resting in shade and sipping water usually helps; tell an adult if he feels very unwell.

scenario: A man has sudden, severe pain that comes in waves from his back and side down towards his groin. His urine looks pink. What is the most likely cause?
optionNotes: Burning pain in the upper belly
Pain settles in the lower right belly
Would be in the leg, not the back
Stone scraping down the ureter; blood in urine
explain: A kidney stone is a hard lump of minerals that forms when urine is concentrated. As it moves down the narrow ureter, the muscles squeeze around it and cause waves of pain from the back to the groin. It can scrape the lining, so a little blood colours the urine pink. Drinking enough water helps prevent stones.

scenario: A doctor wants a quick, painless first check on how a child's kidneys are working. Which test should come first?
optionNotes: Shows what the kidneys are letting through
explain: Urine is made by the kidneys, so it shows what they are doing. A urine test can find things that should not be there, such as blood, protein or sugar. It needs only a small sample collected in a clean cup, so it is a common first test before a blood test or scan.

scenario: Priya's aunt wants to donate a kidney to her brother, whose kidneys have failed. She asks how many kidneys a person needs to live a healthy life. What is the answer?
optionNotes: Without any kidney, waste builds up
One healthy kidney can do the work of two
Most people have two, but one is enough
People normally have two, not three
explain: Most people are born with two kidneys, but one healthy kidney can do enough filtering for the whole body. After a donation, the remaining kidney grows a little and takes on more work. This is why living people can safely donate a kidney after doctors check they are healthy.

scenario: A girl often holds her urine for long hours at school. Now she feels burning when she passes urine and needs to go very often. What is the most likely problem?
optionNotes: Slow, hard poop; no burning urine
Loose, watery poop; no burning urine
Germs in the bladder or urethra
explain: A urinary tract infection happens when germs get into the urethra and bladder. Urine left sitting for long gives germs time to grow, which irritates the lining and causes burning and frequent urges. A doctor may test the urine and prescribe medicine. Drinking enough water and going to the toilet when you need to help prevent it.

scenario: A pathologist tests a healthy child's urine sample. Which substance makes up most of it?
optionNotes: Main waste, but only a small part
Should not be in healthy urine
explain: Urine is about 95% water. Wastes such as urea and extra salts are dissolved in that water, which is how the kidneys carry them out of the body. This is why you need to drink enough: the kidneys need water to wash wastes away. Blood in urine is a sign to see a doctor.

scenario: During a cricket match on a very hot day, a boy feels dizzy, weak and sweaty, with a headache. He is awake and talking. What should be done first?
options: Move him to a cool, shady place and give sips of water
Let him keep playing to finish the match
Wrap him in a warm blanket
Give him a cup of hot tea
answer: Move him to a cool, shady place and give sips of water
optionNotes: Cools the body and replaces lost fluid
More heat and sweating makes it worse
explain: These are signs of heat exhaustion: the body has lost a lot of water and salt through sweat and is struggling to cool down. Move him out of the sun, loosen tight clothes, cool his skin with a damp cloth and give small sips of water or ORS. An adult should stay with him and get medical help if he does not improve or becomes confused.

scenario: A blood test shows a patient has high levels of urea and creatinine in her blood. Which organs are most likely not working well?
optionNotes: Should remove urea and creatinine into urine
explain: Urea comes from breaking down protein, and creatinine comes from working muscles. Healthy kidneys keep both at low levels by moving them into urine. If they build up in the blood, it suggests the kidneys are not filtering well. A nephrologist, a kidney doctor, would then look for the cause.

scenario: A doctor wants a painless picture of a child's kidneys that uses sound waves and no radiation. Which test is this?
optionNotes: Sound echoes build a live picture
explain: An ultrasound sends very high-pitched sound, too high for us to hear, into the body. The sound bounces off organs, and a computer turns the echoes into a picture. It uses no radiation, so it is safe for children and is the same kind of scan used to see babies before birth. It can show the size of the kidneys and stones or blockages.

scenario: In class, a student asks a kidney doctor how big a kidney is. Which comparison is closest?
optionNotes: About 10 to 12 cm long in an adult
explain: Each adult kidney is about 10 to 12 cm long, roughly the size of a fist. Even though kidneys are small, they receive about a fifth of all the blood the heart pumps each minute. That huge blood flow lets them clean all your blood many times every day.

scenario: Tara has a sore throat. The doctor feels small, tender lumps on both sides of her neck, below the jaw. These lumps usually go down when the infection clears. What are they?
optionNotes: Single gland at the front of the neck
Not linked to a throat infection
Swell in mumps, near the ears
explain: Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped filters along lymph vessels. When germs are nearby, white blood cells in the nodes multiply to fight them, so the nodes swell and feel tender. Once the infection clears, they shrink back. Lumps that stay large for weeks should be checked by a doctor.

scenario: A bodybuilder eats far more protein than his body needs. The extra amino acids are broken down. Which waste will his kidneys have to remove more of?
optionNotes: Made by the liver for digestion
Useful fuel, kept in the blood
Made from the nitrogen in extra protein
explain: The body cannot store extra protein. The amino acids are broken down, and the nitrogen in them becomes ammonia, which the liver turns into urea. More protein eaten means more urea in the blood for the kidneys to remove, and the body needs more water to flush it out.

scenario: After drinking two big glasses of water, Neha feels a strong urge to go to the toilet. Which organ is stretching and sending signals to her brain?
optionNotes: Makes urine but does not store it
explain: Kidneys make urine all the time, and it drips down the ureters into the bladder. The bladder's muscular wall stretches as it fills. Nerves in the wall send messages to the brain, which you feel as the urge to go. A ring of muscle keeps urine in until you reach a toilet.

scenario: A patient's skin and the whites of his eyes have turned yellow. His doctor explains that a yellow waste from old red blood cells is building up because one organ is not clearing it. Which organ?
optionNotes: Clears the yellow pigment into bile
Mainly removes urea; not the main exit for this pigment
explain: When old red blood cells are broken down, a yellow pigment called bilirubin is made. The liver normally collects it and sends it out in bile. If the liver is unwell or bile cannot flow, bilirubin builds up and turns skin and eyes yellow. This is called jaundice, and a doctor needs to find the cause.
fact: Many newborn babies get mild jaundice for a few days because their liver is still getting up to speed.

scenario: A school poster shows a urine colour chart. Which colour shows a person is drinking about the right amount?
optionNotes: Badly dehydrated or unwell: see a doctor
Very concentrated: drink more; see a doctor if it stays
explain: Urine gets its yellow colour from a pigment the body makes when it recycles old red blood cells. With plenty of water, the pigment is diluted and urine looks pale straw yellow. With too little water, the kidneys save water and urine gets darker. Red or brown urine needs a doctor's check.

scenario: On a hot day, Kiran sweats a lot and notices he goes to the toilet much less often than usual. What is the best explanation?
options: All his urine is coming out as sweat
optionNotes: They take back more water into the blood
The bladder only stores what it receives
Blockage causes pain, not a hot-day pattern
Sweat and urine are made in different places
explain: When you lose water as sweat, your brain releases a hormone that tells the kidneys to take back more water from the tubules into the blood. Less urine is made, and it is darker. This keeps your body's water level steady. Drinking more water on hot days lets the kidneys return to normal.

notes: Take in oxygen when you breathe
Tube carrying food to the stomach
Bag that churns food with acid
Long tube where nutrients are absorbed
reason: Lungs belong to the breathing system; the rest are on the food's path.
explain: Food travels through one long tube: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine. Each part has a job, from chewing to absorbing nutrients. The lungs sit in the chest too, but they handle air, not food. They belong to the breathing system.
fact: If you laid out an adult's whole digestive tube, it would be about 9 metres long.

notes: Lump of tissue at the back of the throat
reason: Tonsils are not teeth; the other four are types of teeth.
explain: You have four kinds of teeth, each shaped for a job. Incisors cut, canines tear, and premolars and molars crush and grind food into small pieces. Smaller pieces are easier for digestive juices to work on. Tonsils are soft lumps at the back of the throat that help catch germs.
fact: Children have 20 milk teeth; adults have up to 32 permanent teeth.

notes: Made from milk, rich in protein
Made from wheat flour, mostly starch
Made from wheat flour, mostly starch
reason: Paneer is a protein food; the rest are grain foods rich in carbohydrates.
explain: Rice, chapati, oats and bread are made from grains. Grains are rich in carbohydrates, mainly starch, which your body breaks into glucose for energy. Paneer is made from milk and gives you protein, which your body uses to build and repair itself.

notes: Made from soybeans, very high in protein
reason: Sugar is a carbohydrate with no protein; the others are protein foods.
explain: Proteins are body-building foods. Your body breaks them into small units called amino acids and uses them to make muscle, skin, hair and enzymes. Egg, dal, fish and soya are all good protein sources. Sugar gives quick energy but no protein, vitamins or minerals.

notes: Stomach enzyme that breaks down protein
Pancreas enzyme that breaks down protein
reason: Insulin is a hormone; the other four are digestive enzymes.
explain: Digestive enzymes are chemical helpers that cut big food molecules into small ones your body can absorb. Amylase works on starch, pepsin and trypsin work on protein, and lipase works on fat. Insulin is a hormone carried in the blood. It does not digest food; it helps cells take in sugar.
fact: Most enzyme names end in '-ase', which makes them easy to spot.

notes: Makes bile; food never passes through
reason: Food never travels through the liver; it passes through all the others.
explain: The digestive system has two kinds of parts. The gut tube is the path food actually travels through. Helper organs such as the liver and pancreas sit beside the tube and send in juices. The liver makes bile, which flows into the small intestine to help digest fat, but no food goes inside the liver.

reason: Goitre comes from too little iodine (a mineral); the rest come from too little of a vitamin.
explain: A deficiency disease happens when your diet is missing a nutrient for a long time. Scurvy, rickets, night blindness and beriberi are each caused by missing a vitamin. Goitre, a swelling in the neck, is usually caused by missing iodine, which is a mineral. That is why salt in India is sold with iodine added.
fact: Beriberi spread in places where people ate mostly polished white rice, because polishing removes vitamin B1.

notes: Dissolves in fat, stored in the liver
Dissolves in water, not stored much
Dissolves in fat, stored in the body
Dissolves in fat, stored in the body
Dissolves in fat, helps blood clot
reason: Vitamin C dissolves in water; A, D, E and K dissolve in fat.
explain: Vitamins come in two groups. Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat, so your body can store them in the liver and fat for later. Vitamin C (and the B vitamins) dissolve in water. Any extra leaves in your urine, so you need some almost every day from fruit and vegetables.

notes: Fruit with fibre, especially in the skin
Whole grain with its fibre kept
reason: Butter has no fibre; the other four are good sources of fibre.
explain: Fibre is the part of plant food your body cannot digest. It still matters: it adds bulk so waste moves smoothly through the large intestine. Fruit, vegetables, beans and whole grains all contain fibre. Butter is a fat from milk and has none.

notes: Strong acid in the stomach that kills germs
Tiny fingers lining the small intestine
Slimy layer protecting the stomach wall
Mix of juices made by the stomach
reason: Villi are in the small intestine; the rest are found in the stomach.
explain: The stomach makes gastric juice, which contains hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin. The acid kills many germs and helps pepsin start breaking down protein. A thick layer of mucus stops the stomach from digesting its own wall. Villi are found further on, in the small intestine, where they absorb nutrients.

notes: No enzymes; breaks fat into droplets
Has enzymes for starch, protein and fat
reason: Bile has no enzymes; the other four juices contain digestive enzymes.
explain: Most digestive juices contain enzymes that chemically break food apart. Bile, made by the liver, works differently. It breaks big blobs of fat into tiny droplets, the way soap breaks up grease. This gives the fat-digesting enzyme lipase much more fat surface to work on.
fact: Bile is what gives poop its brown colour, after gut bacteria change its pigments.

notes: Mineral for carrying oxygen in blood
Mineral for healing and fighting infection
reason: Glucose is a sugar (carbohydrate); the others are minerals.
explain: Minerals are simple substances from the earth that your body needs in small amounts. Iron helps blood carry oxygen, calcium builds bones and teeth, iodine helps the thyroid gland, and zinc helps wounds heal. Glucose is a sugar your body gets by digesting carbohydrates, and cells burn it for energy.

notes: Big molecule that still needs digesting
reason: Starch is a big food molecule; the others are small end products of digestion.
explain: Digestion turns big food molecules into small ones that can pass through the gut wall into your blood. Starch is broken into glucose, proteins into amino acids, and fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Starch itself is too big to be absorbed, so it must be digested first.

notes: Liver job: stores vitamins for later
reason: Insulin is made by the pancreas; the other four are jobs of the liver.
explain: The liver is your largest internal organ and does hundreds of jobs. It makes bile for fat digestion, stores extra sugar as glycogen, keeps a store of vitamins like A, and makes proteins that help blood clot. Insulin is made in the pancreas, a separate organ that sits behind the stomach.
fact: The liver can regrow lost parts. A person can donate part of their liver and it grows back.

notes: Removes food and germs from teeth
Feeds germs that make tooth-eating acid
reason: Sipping sugary drinks harms teeth; the rest protect them.
explain: Germs in your mouth feed on sugar and make acid. The acid slowly dissolves enamel, the hard outer coat of a tooth, and makes holes called cavities. Sipping sugar all day keeps the acid attack going for hours. Brushing, flossing, rinsing and dental check-ups remove germs and food and catch problems early.

notes: Chemical: enzyme changes starch into sugar
Physical: breaks food into smaller pieces
Physical: rolls food into a ball
Physical: splits fat into small blobs
reason: Amylase digests food chemically; the others break or mix food physically.
explain: There are two kinds of digestion. Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces without changing what it is made of, like chewing or bile splitting fat into droplets. Chemical digestion uses enzymes to change big molecules into new, smaller ones. Amylase turns starch into sugar, so it is chemical.
fact: Chew a plain piece of roti for a minute and it starts to taste slightly sweet. That is amylase making sugar.

notes: Hole in a tooth from acid
reason: Asthma affects the lungs; the others affect the digestive system.
explain: Your digestive system runs from your teeth to your bottom, so problems anywhere along it count. Cavities affect teeth, ulcers affect the stomach lining, and constipation and diarrhoea happen when the intestines move waste too slowly or too fast. Asthma is a lung problem, where airways become narrow.

clues: Your body makes about a litre or more of this every day without you noticing.
It contains an enzyme that starts turning starch into sugar.
It wets your food so you can chew and swallow, and you make more when you smell something tasty.
explain: Saliva is the first digestive juice. Glands around your mouth make it. It softens food so you can swallow, and its enzyme, amylase, starts breaking starch into sugar. Just thinking about tasty food can make your glands release more.
fact: Without saliva you could not taste food, because taste buds can only detect chemicals dissolved in liquid.

clues: This muscular tube is about 25 centimetres long in an adult.
Rings of muscle squeeze in waves to push each mouthful down, even if you are upside down.
It runs behind the windpipe, down through your chest, to the organ where acid digestion begins.
explain: The oesophagus, or food pipe, carries food from the throat to the stomach. It does not digest food; it moves it, using waves of muscle squeezing called peristalsis. A small flap called the epiglottis covers the windpipe when you swallow, so food goes into the oesophagus and not your lungs.

clues: It works even when you eat lying down or hanging upside down.
Rings in the gut wall tighten behind a lump of food and relax in front of it.
It moves food along the whole digestive tube, like toothpaste moving along when you press its tube.
explain: Peristalsis is the wave-like squeezing of muscles in the walls of your gut. The muscle behind the food tightens while the muscle in front relaxes, so food is pushed forward. Gravity is not needed. It moves food from the oesophagus all the way to the end of the large intestine.

clues: Millions of them line the inside walls of the longest part of your gut.
Each one has tiny blood vessels inside to carry nutrients away.
These tiny bumps stick out like the loops on a fluffy towel, giving much more area to take in digested food.
explain: Villi are tiny finger-like bumps on the inner wall of the small intestine. They greatly increase the surface area, so digested food can pass into the blood much faster. Each villus has thin walls and a network of blood vessels close to the surface, so nutrients only travel a tiny distance.
fact: The folds and villi of the small intestine give it an inside area of about 30 square metres, many times more than a smooth tube would have.

clues: This juice has no enzymes, yet some foods would be digested slowly without it.
It is stored in a small pouch and squirted into the first part of the small intestine after a meal.
It breaks oily food into tiny droplets, the way dish soap breaks up grease on a plate.
explain: Bile is a yellow-green juice made by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It contains no enzymes. It breaks large fat globules into tiny droplets, which gives the fat-digesting enzyme lipase more surface to work on. This is called emulsification.

clues: Pepsin, lipase and trypsin are examples.
Each one fits only certain molecules, like a key fits only one lock.
These chemical helpers cut big food molecules into small ones quickly and are not used up.
explain: An enzyme is a substance that makes a chemical change happen much faster. Digestive enzymes cut big molecules such as starch, protein and fat into small pieces the body can absorb. Each enzyme works on one kind of food molecule, and it can be used again and again.

clues: This small, finger-shaped tube hangs off the start of the large intestine.
Scientists think it may store helpful gut bacteria, but people live normally without it.
If it gets blocked and swollen, it causes belly pain and usually has to be taken out.
explain: The appendix is a narrow tube, about the length of a finger, attached to the large intestine on the lower right of the belly. Its job is still being studied; it may be a store of good bacteria. If it becomes blocked and infected (appendicitis), doctors usually remove it in an operation.

clues: Adults have twelve of these, including four that can arrive late, called wisdom ones.
Their wide, bumpy tops crush food into a soft paste.
They are the last ones in each row, farthest from your lips.
explain: Molars are the large, flat-topped teeth at the back of your mouth. Their wide surfaces crush and grind food into small pieces, which gives digestive juices more food surface to work on. Adults have 12 molars, including the 4 wisdom teeth.

clues: It is the toughest material your body makes, tougher than bone.
Acid made by germs feeding on sugar can dissolve it and make holes.
Fluoride in the paste you use each morning and night helps protect this shiny outer coat.
explain: Enamel is the outer layer of a tooth and the hardest substance in the body. It has no living cells, so once acid wears a hole in it, it cannot repair itself. That is why cavities need a dentist to fill them. Fluoride makes enamel more resistant to acid.

clues: Your body cannot digest this part of plant food, but you still need it.
Whole grains, beans, and fruit eaten with the skin have plenty of it.
It adds bulk and helps waste move smoothly through the large intestine.
explain: Fibre, also called roughage, comes from the walls of plant cells. Human enzymes cannot break it down, so it passes through the gut. On the way it holds water and adds bulk, which helps the intestine muscles move waste along and prevents constipation.

clues: Your digestive juices break it into small units called amino acids.
Hair, nails, skin and enzymes are all made from it.
Paneer, fish, beans and milk are good sources for growing children.
explain: Protein is the body's building material. Digestion breaks it into amino acids, which your body then joins together in new ways to build muscle, skin, hair, enzymes and antibodies. Growing children need protein every day because the body cannot store much of it.

clues: Your saliva begins to digest this nutrient while you chew.
It is broken down into glucose, which your cells burn as fuel.
Roti, potatoes, bread and bananas are rich in it.
explain: Carbohydrates are the body's main source of energy. They include starches in grains and potatoes and sugars in fruit. Digestion breaks them into glucose, which travels in the blood to every cell. Cells use glucose to power everything from thinking to running.

clues: Long ago this disease was common on long sea voyages with no fresh food.
Without a certain nutrient, the body cannot make strong connecting tissue, so wounds heal slowly.
Eating lemons, amla or guava prevents it.
explain: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C. The body needs vitamin C to make collagen, a protein that holds skin, gums and blood vessels together. Without it, gums bleed and cuts heal slowly. Fresh fruit and vegetables prevent and cure it.
fact: Amla (Indian gooseberry) has far more vitamin C than an orange of the same weight.

clues: Its name comes from a language spoken in Ghana.
It often appears when a young child stops breastfeeding and then eats mostly starchy food.
Fluid collects in the legs and tummy, while the arms stay thin.
explain: Kwashiorkor is a disease caused by too little protein in the diet, even if the child gets some energy from starchy food. Protein in the blood helps hold water inside blood vessels. When protein is low, fluid leaks out and gathers in the tummy and legs. Marasmus is different: it comes from too little food of every kind.

clues: Not eating enough fibre or drinking enough water can lead to this.
Waste moves too slowly through the large intestine, which keeps soaking water out of it.
You go fewer times than usual and it can feel uncomfortable to push.
explain: The large intestine takes water back from waste. When waste moves slowly, too much water is removed and it becomes hard and dry. Eating fibre, drinking enough water and being active all help keep waste soft and moving.

clues: Most cases are caused by a germ called H. pylori or by taking some medicines for aches too often, not by spicy food.
It is an open wound in the inner lining of the digestive tract.
Doctors can see it with a thin camera tube passed down the throat.
explain: An ulcer is an open sore in the lining of the stomach or the first part of the small intestine. Normally a mucus layer protects the lining from stomach acid. A germ called H. pylori, or some painkillers, can damage that layer so acid eats into the wall. Doctors treat it with medicines that lower acid and, if needed, kill the germ.

clues: It sits on the upper right side of your belly, under the ribs.
It stores extra sugar as glycogen and keeps some vitamins for later.
It makes a yellow-green juice that is kept in the gall bladder and helps break up fat.
explain: The liver is the largest organ inside your body. In digestion it makes bile, which helps break up fat. It also stores sugar as glycogen, stores vitamins and iron, and changes harmful substances into safer ones. All the blood coming from the intestines passes through the liver first.

scenario: Ravi eats toffees every day and often skips brushing at night. Now one back tooth has a dark spot and hurts when he drinks something cold. What is the most likely problem?
optionNotes: Acid from germs has made a hole in the enamel
Would follow an injury, with swelling
Sore throat, not a sore tooth
Bleeding gums from too little vitamin C
explain: Mouth germs feed on sugar left on teeth and make acid. Over time the acid dissolves enamel and makes a hole, called a cavity. Once the hole reaches the softer layer inside, cold or sweet food causes pain. A dentist cleans out the decay and fills the hole; brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste helps prevent it.

scenario: A patient has not eaten any fruit or fresh vegetables for months. Her gums bleed easily and small cuts take a long time to heal. Which vitamin is she most likely missing?
optionNotes: Lack causes poor sight in dim light
Lack causes scurvy: bleeding gums, slow healing
Needed for blood clotting, not gum healing
explain: Vitamin C is needed to make collagen, a protein that holds gums, skin and blood vessels together. Without it, gums bleed and wounds heal slowly. This disease is called scurvy. Fruits like amla, guava, oranges and lemons, and many vegetables, are rich in vitamin C.

scenario: Meera eats mostly white bread, biscuits and chips, and drinks very little water. She goes to the toilet only twice a week, and it is hard and painful. What is the best advice?
options: Eat more fruit, vegetables and whole grains, and drink more water
Eat more chips so food passes faster
Skip breakfast to rest the stomach
Drink less water so the gut is not overloaded
answer: Eat more fruit, vegetables and whole grains, and drink more water
optionNotes: Fibre and water keep waste soft and moving
Chips have little fibre and lots of salt
Skipping meals does not help constipation
Less water makes waste even harder
explain: Meera has constipation. Her large intestine is soaking too much water out of slow-moving waste. Fibre from plant foods holds water and adds bulk, which helps intestine muscles push waste along. Drinking enough water and staying active help too.

scenario: A young child rarely goes outdoors and drinks very little milk. Her leg bones have started to bend outward, and her bones feel soft. Which nutrient is she most likely missing?
optionNotes: Helps the gut absorb calcium for bones
Lack causes tiredness and pale skin
Helps the gut move waste, not bone strength
explain: This is rickets. Bones need calcium to become hard, and vitamin D helps the intestine absorb calcium from food. Your skin makes vitamin D when sunlight falls on it, and some foods like milk, eggs and fish provide it too. Without enough, growing bones stay soft and bend under the body's weight.
fact: A short time in the sun most days helps the skin make vitamin D.

scenario: A boy can see well in daylight but struggles to see anything in a dim room or at dusk. His diet has almost no carrots, green leafy vegetables, eggs or milk. Which vitamin should he get more of?
optionNotes: Needed to see in dim light
explain: Your eyes use vitamin A to make a pigment that detects dim light. Without enough vitamin A, seeing in low light becomes hard. This is called night blindness. Carrots, mangoes, papaya and green leafy vegetables contain a substance the body turns into vitamin A; milk and eggs provide it directly.

scenario: A man has had burning pain in his upper belly for weeks. A camera test shows a small open wound in his stomach lining, and a test finds the germ H. pylori. What condition does he have?
optionNotes: Swollen appendix, pain in lower right belly
Hard lumps in the gall bladder
Slow-moving waste in the large intestine
Open sore in the stomach lining
explain: A stomach ulcer is an open sore in the stomach lining. Normally mucus protects the lining from strong stomach acid. The germ H. pylori can damage that protection, letting acid hurt the wall. Doctors treat it with medicines to kill the germ and lower acid, and the sore heals.

scenario: A girl's belly pain began near her belly button and moved to the lower right side. She has a fever, feels sick, and it hurts more when she walks. Which organ is most likely swollen?
optionNotes: Sits in the upper right, under the liver
Small tube at the lower right; classic pattern
Sits in the upper right, under the ribs
explain: This is the classic pattern of appendicitis: pain that starts around the belly button and shifts to the lower right, with fever and feeling sick. The appendix is a small tube on the large intestine in the lower right belly. If it is blocked and infected, doctors usually remove it with an operation before it can burst.

scenario: A woman has gallstones blocking the tube that carries bile into her small intestine. She gets pain after oily meals. Digestion of which nutrient is most affected?
optionNotes: Digested by amylase from saliva and pancreas
Needs bile to break into droplets first
explain: Bile breaks large blobs of fat into tiny droplets so the enzyme lipase can digest them quickly. When gallstones block bile from reaching the intestine, fat is poorly digested. Oily meals also make the gall bladder squeeze against the blockage, which causes pain.

scenario: After eating at a wedding, a boy has vomiting and watery diarrhoea several times. He is tired and his mouth is dry. While an adult takes him to a doctor, what helps most?
options: Small, frequent sips of ORS solution
No drinks at all until tomorrow
A big, spicy meal to regain strength
answer: Small, frequent sips of ORS solution
optionNotes: Too much sugar can worsen diarrhoea
Hard to keep down and irritates the gut
explain: Vomiting and diarrhoea make the body lose water and salts fast, which can lead to dehydration. ORS (oral rehydration solution) has the right mix of water, salt and a little sugar, so the gut absorbs it well. Small, frequent sips are easier to keep down than big gulps. A doctor should check a child with these symptoms.
fact: ORS has been estimated to save millions of children's lives, using just water, salt and sugar.

scenario: A dentist tells Anu to brush twice a day with a toothpaste containing a mineral that makes tooth enamel stronger against acid. Which mineral is it?
optionNotes: Strengthens enamel and helps resist acid
explain: Enamel is attacked by acid made when mouth germs eat sugar. Fluoride joins into the enamel surface and makes it harder for acid to dissolve. It can also help repair very early weak spots before they become holes. Children should use only a small, pea-sized amount of toothpaste and spit it out.

scenario: Every time Kabir drinks a glass of milk he gets a bloated tummy, gas and loose motions. Roti, rice and fruit cause no trouble. His body makes too little of the enzyme for which sugar?
optionNotes: Already a single small sugar, needs no digesting
The sugar in milk, digested by lactase
Found in roti and rice, which are fine
explain: This is lactose intolerance. Lactose is the natural sugar in milk, and the enzyme lactase splits it so it can be absorbed. Without enough lactase, lactose reaches the large intestine undigested. Gut bacteria feed on it there and make gas, causing bloating and loose motions. Curd and some cheeses usually have less lactose and may be easier to eat.

scenario: A girl is recovering from a broken arm and is also growing fast. Her body needs to build and repair tissues. Which nutrient should she make sure she eats enough of?
optionNotes: Body-building nutrient for growth and repair
explain: Protein is digested into amino acids, which the body uses as building blocks for new muscle, skin, blood and repair of injuries. Growing children and people healing from injuries need more of it. Dal, eggs, milk, paneer, fish, beans and nuts are good sources. Her bones also need calcium and vitamin D.

scenario: A patient had a large part of his small intestine removed after an illness. He now eats well but keeps losing weight. Which job of the gut is most likely affected?
optionNotes: Main job of the small intestine and its villi
Done by glands around the mouth
Done by teeth in the mouth
explain: Most digested food is absorbed in the small intestine. Its walls are covered in villi, tiny fingers that give a huge area for nutrients to pass into the blood. With less small intestine, there is less area for absorption, so much of the food leaves the body before it can be taken in.

scenario: After a large, oily dinner, a man lies down straight away and feels a burning feeling behind his breastbone with a sour taste. Stomach acid has moved up into which part?
optionNotes: Carries air, protected by a flap
A muscle pump, not part of the food path
Food pipe just above the stomach
Air organs, not on the food path
explain: A ring of muscle at the top of the stomach usually stops acid from flowing back up. A big meal and lying down soon after can let acid leak into the oesophagus, which lacks the stomach's thick protective mucus layer. This causes heartburn, even though the heart is not involved. Smaller meals and waiting a couple of hours before lying down help.

scenario: Four friends compare their school lunches. Which lunch is the most balanced?
options: Roti, dal, vegetable sabzi and curd
answer: Roti, dal, vegetable sabzi and curd
optionNotes: Carbohydrate, protein, vitamins, minerals and fibre
Vitamins and fibre, but little protein
explain: A balanced diet gives you every nutrient in the right amounts: carbohydrates and fats for energy, protein for growth, vitamins and minerals for health, plus fibre and water. Roti gives carbohydrates, dal and curd give protein and calcium, and vegetables give vitamins, minerals and fibre. No single food provides everything.

scenario: A doctor wants to look directly at the inside of a patient's stomach to check for a sore. Which test lets the doctor see it?
optionNotes: Shows bones and lungs, not stomach lining
Thin tube with a camera passed down the throat
explain: An endoscope is a thin, bendy tube with a light and a tiny camera at its tip. It is passed gently through the mouth and oesophagus into the stomach, while the patient is given medicine to stay comfortable. The doctor sees the lining on a screen and can take a tiny sample if needed. X-rays show dense things like bone well, but not the soft lining of the stomach.

notes: Tiny germs that copy inside cells
Your own cells that carry oxygen
Moulds and yeasts; some cause infections
reason: Red blood cells are part of your body; the other four are kinds of germs.
explain: Germs are microbes, too small to see without a microscope, that can cause disease. The main kinds are bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa, such as the parasite that causes malaria. Red blood cells are not germs; they are your own cells that carry oxygen around your body.

notes: Bacteria; spread by dirty food and water
reason: Typhoid is caused by bacteria; the other four are caused by viruses.
explain: Doctors group diseases by the kind of germ that causes them, because that decides the treatment. Chickenpox, flu, measles and dengue are caused by viruses. Typhoid is caused by bacteria, usually spread through dirty food or water, which is why antibiotics can treat it but cannot treat the other four.

reason: Cholera spreads through dirty water; the other four are spread by mosquitoes.
explain: Some germs need a carrier to move from person to person. Mosquitoes pick up the germs of malaria, dengue, chikungunya and yellow fever when they bite a sick person and pass them on with the next bite. Cholera spreads when drinking water or food is dirtied with sewage. Removing standing water stops mosquitoes breeding, while clean water and toilets stop cholera.
fact: Only female mosquitoes bite; they need blood to make their eggs.

notes: Spread through the air by coughing
Spread by dirty food and water
Liver infection from dirty food or water
reason: Tuberculosis spreads through the air; the other four spread through dirty food or water.
explain: Knowing how a germ travels tells you how to stop it. Cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A and food poisoning spread when food or water is dirtied with germs, so clean water, hand washing and safe cooking prevent them. Tuberculosis (TB) spreads through tiny droplets in the air when a person with TB of the lungs coughs, so it needs different protection.

notes: Wash germs out of the eyes
reason: Insulin controls blood sugar; the other four defend the body against germs.
explain: Your body has layers of defence. Skin is a wall, sticky mucus in the nose traps germs, and tears wash the eyes and contain germ-killing substances. If germs still get in, white blood cells attack them. Insulin is a hormone that controls blood sugar and has no role in fighting germs.

notes: Magnet shows soft parts in detail
Lab checks a sample of blood
X-rays from many angles make slices
Sound waves show organs and unborn babies
reason: A blood test studies a sample in a lab; the other four make pictures of the inside of the body.
explain: Imaging tests let doctors see inside the body without surgery. X-rays and CT scans use X-rays, MRI uses a strong magnet and radio waves, and ultrasound uses sound waves. A blood test makes no picture: a small sample is taken and checked in a laboratory for things like germs, sugar or the number of blood cells.

notes: Uses a magnet and radio waves
reason: MRI uses a magnet and radio waves; the other four use X-rays.
explain: X-rays are invisible rays that pass through soft parts but are blocked by bones and teeth, which show up white on the picture. A CT scan uses X-rays too, taken from many angles and joined by a computer into slices. An MRI scan uses no X-rays at all: a very strong magnet and radio waves make detailed pictures, especially of soft parts like the brain and muscles.

notes: Expert who prepares and gives out medicines
reason: A pharmacist is a medicines expert; the other four are doctors who examine and treat patients.
explain: Doctors examine patients, find out what is wrong and decide on treatment. Many specialise in one part of the body or one age group. A pharmacist is a different health expert who checks a doctor's prescription, prepares the medicine and explains how to take it safely.

notes: Wrong: neurologists treat brain and nerves
reason: A neurologist treats the brain and nerves, not bones; the other four pairs are correct.
explain: A specialist's name often comes from Greek words for the body part. 'Cardio' means heart, 'ophthalmo' means eye, 'derma' means skin, 'nephro' means kidney and 'neuro' means nerve. Bones and joints are treated by an orthopaedic doctor.
fact: The ending '-ologist' means 'someone who studies'.

notes: Bacteria; fluids first, antibiotics may help
reason: The common cold is caused by viruses, so antibiotics do not help; the other four are bacterial infections.
explain: Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them multiplying. They work by attacking parts that bacteria have, such as their cell wall. Viruses do not have those parts, so antibiotics have no effect on a cold. A cold gets better on its own with rest and fluids.

reason: Sharing a toothbrush spreads germs; the other four stop germs spreading.
explain: Germs move from person to person on hands, in droplets from coughs, in dirty water and on shared objects. Soap washes germs off, covering coughs blocks droplets, boiling kills germs in water, and having your own towel keeps germs to yourself. A toothbrush carries germs from your mouth and gums, so sharing one passes them to someone else.

notes: Not caused by a germ; no vaccine
Prevented by drops or a shot
reason: Diabetes is not caused by a germ and has no vaccine; the other four are prevented by vaccines.
explain: A vaccine trains your immune system to recognise a particular germ before you ever meet it. Polio, measles, tetanus and hepatitis B are all caused by germs, and children in India get vaccines against them. Diabetes is a problem with the hormone insulin, not an infection, so no vaccine can prevent it.
fact: India was declared free of polio in 2014, thanks largely to mass vaccination.

reason: The malaria parasite causes disease; the other four microbes are useful to people.
explain: Most microbes are harmless and many are useful. Bacteria turn milk into curd, yeast makes dough rise, the mould Penicillium gave us penicillin, and bacteria in the roots of pea and bean plants add nitrogen to the soil. Only a few microbes cause disease, such as the parasite that causes malaria.

notes: Fungus; white patches in the mouth
reason: Chickenpox is caused by a virus; the other four are fungal infections.
explain: Some fungi can grow on the skin, nails or inside the mouth, especially where it is warm and damp. Ringworm is caused by a fungus, not a worm; it gets its name from its ring shape. Fungal infections are treated with antifungal medicine. Chickenpox is caused by a virus and spreads through the air and by touch.

reason: A dry scab is a normal sign of healing; the other four can be signs that a wound is infected.
explain: When germs get into a wound, the body sends extra blood and white blood cells to fight them. This causes redness, swelling and warmth, and dead white cells and germs collect as pus. A dry scab is the body's natural plaster that protects new skin growing underneath. An adult should show an infected wound to a doctor.

items: Take only if a doctor prescribes
reason: Saving leftover antibiotics is unsafe; the other four are correct rules for taking them.
explain: If antibiotics are stopped early or used when they are not needed, the toughest bacteria can survive and multiply. Over time this creates bacteria that antibiotics cannot kill, called antibiotic resistance. Taking the full course exactly as prescribed, and never using leftovers, helps keep these medicines working.

notes: Made the first vaccine, for smallpox
Showed germs cause disease and spoiling
reason: Isaac Newton was a physicist; the other four made discoveries about germs and disease.
explain: Our fight against germs was built step by step. Jenner made the first vaccine in 1796, Pasteur showed that microbes cause disease and spoil food, Ross proved in 1897, while working in India, that mosquitoes carry malaria, and Fleming discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic. Newton was a famous scientist too, but he studied physics.
fact: Ronald Ross won the Nobel Prize in 1902 for his malaria work.

clues: Edward Jenner made the first one in 1796, using material from cowpox sores.
It contains a weakened, killed or harmless piece of a germ, so the body can practise fighting it.
Babies get several of these, some as drops in the mouth and many as shots, to stay safe from polio and measles.
explain: A vaccine shows your immune system a harmless version or piece of a germ. Your body makes antibodies and memory cells against it, without you getting ill. If the real germ arrives later, the body recognises it and fights it off quickly. Antibiotics kill bacteria that are already causing an infection; vaccines prevent infection in the first place.

clues: Taking too many of these, or stopping them too early, can help germs become resistant.
It kills or stops microbes like those causing typhoid or TB, but does nothing against viruses.
Alexander Fleming discovered the first one, made by a mould, in 1928.
explain: Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them multiplying. They do not work on viruses such as colds and flu. Using them wrongly lets resistant bacteria survive and spread, so they should only be taken when a doctor prescribes them, for the full course.

clues: A mother passes some of these to her baby through breast milk.
Each kind is Y-shaped and fits only one particular invader, like a key in a lock.
Your body makes them after an infection or a vaccine, and they stick to invaders to mark them for destruction.
explain: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins made by certain white blood cells. Each one fits a particular germ, sticks to it and flags it for other cells to destroy. After an infection or vaccine, the body remembers how to make that antibody, so it can respond fast next time. Antibiotics are medicines; antibodies are made by your own body.

clues: Pus is made mostly of these, after they have done their job.
Some of them swallow invaders whole; others make antibodies.
These cells, made in the bone marrow, are the body's soldiers against microbes.
explain: White blood cells are the body's defence force. They travel in the blood and can leave it to reach any place where germs have entered. Some swallow and digest germs, while others make antibodies. A blood test showing many more white blood cells than usual often means the body is fighting an infection.

clues: It is so small that it can only be seen with a special electron microscope.
It cannot multiply on its own; it must get inside a living cell and use it to make copies.
Chickenpox, measles and dengue are caused by this type of microbe, and antibiotics do not work on it.
explain: A virus is much smaller than a bacterium. It is just genetic instructions wrapped in a coat of protein, and it can only multiply inside a living cell, which it takes over to make copies of itself. Antibiotics cannot harm viruses. Vaccines, and in some cases antiviral medicines, are used against them.

clues: Ronald Ross worked out how it spreads while working in India in 1897.
Its germ lives inside red blood cells and bursts them, causing shivering and a high temperature every few days.
It is passed on by the bite of an infected female Anopheles insect.
explain: Malaria is caused by a single-celled parasite called Plasmodium. An infected female Anopheles mosquito injects it with a bite. It multiplies in the liver, then in red blood cells, bursting them in cycles, which causes repeated bouts of fever and chills. It is diagnosed with a blood test and treated with medicines; bed nets and removing standing water help prevent it.

clues: Cases rise during and after the monsoon, when water collects in pots, tyres and coolers.
It causes a high temperature, severe body ache and pain behind the eyes.
It is a viral illness spread by striped insects that bite during the day.
explain: Dengue is caused by a virus carried by the striped Aedes mosquito, which breeds in small pools of clean standing water and bites in the daytime. There is no medicine that kills the virus, so doctors give rest and fluids and watch the platelet count closely. Emptying water from coolers, pots and tyres each week helps prevent it.

clues: It is caused by a slow-growing bacterium, and treatment usually lasts at least six months.
It spreads through tiny droplets in the air and often causes night sweats and weight loss.
It mostly attacks the organs of breathing, and babies in India get a vaccine against it soon after birth.
explain: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by bacteria that grow very slowly, so treatment needs several medicines taken every day for six months or more. It usually affects the lungs and spreads when an infected person coughs. TB can be cured if the full course is completed. Babies in India receive the BCG vaccine at birth.

clues: Years later, the same virus can wake up and cause a painful illness called shingles.
It spreads very easily, and a vaccine against it is available.
It causes a mild temperature and many small, fluid-filled bumps that crust over, usually in children.
explain: Chickenpox is caused by a virus that spreads through the air and by touching the fluid in the blisters. The blisters crust over in about a week. Children with it should stay home until all the blisters have crusted. The virus stays asleep in nerves afterwards and can return in adults as shingles.

clues: In 1854, John Snow traced an outbreak in London to one public pump.
Its bacteria spread when sewage gets into wells, ponds or pipes used for drinking.
It causes sudden, severe loose motions, and oral rehydration solution can save the patient's life.
explain: Cholera is caused by bacteria that spread through drinking water dirtied with sewage. It causes so much diarrhoea that the body can lose water dangerously fast. Oral rehydration solution (ORS), a mix of clean water, salt and sugar, replaces what is lost and saves most patients. Clean water and toilets prevent it.
fact: John Snow's map of cholera cases is one of the first uses of maps to track a disease.

clues: Wilhelm Roentgen discovered these invisible rays in 1895.
Dentists use small ones to spot hidden cavities between teeth.
This test shows hard parts of the body as white shapes on a dark film.
explain: X-rays are invisible rays that pass easily through skin and muscle but are blocked by bone and teeth. So hard parts show up white and soft parts look dark. X-rays are quick and painless and help doctors spot broken bones, chest infections and swallowed metal objects. The dose is small, but doctors still use them only when needed.

clues: It uses radio waves and a computer, but no X-rays.
Patients must remove metal objects first, and the machine makes loud knocking sounds.
Doctors use it to see soft parts like nerves, muscles and the spinal cord in great detail.
explain: MRI stands for magnetic resonance imaging. The patient lies inside a large tube with a very strong magnet, which works with radio waves to make detailed pictures of soft tissues. It uses no X-rays, but metal must be kept away from the magnet. Patients need to lie very still, and the machine is noisy.

clues: It is one way the body makes life harder for germs, and often a sign the immune system is working.
A reading above about 38 degrees Celsius counts as this.
When you have it, your forehead feels warm and you may shiver even under a blanket.
explain: Normal body temperature is about 37 degrees Celsius. When germs invade, the brain raises the body's temperature setting, which slows many germs and speeds up the immune system. You may shiver while the temperature is rising. A fever in a young baby, a very high fever, or one lasting more than a few days needs a doctor.

clues: Ringworm and athlete's foot are caused by these, not by worms.
They grow well in warm, damp places, and many feed on dead things.
This group of living things includes the fluffy growth on stale bread and the tiny cells that make dough rise.
explain: Fungi are a group of living things that includes mushrooms, moulds and yeasts. They cannot make their own food, so they feed on dead or living material. Most are harmless or useful, but a few can infect skin, nails or the mouth, especially where it is warm and damp. Keeping skin clean and dry helps prevent this.

clues: It is why most people catch measles only once in their life.
You can gain it by recovering from an illness or by getting a shot, and it means your body is ready for that germ.
It is your body's ability to fight off a particular infection before it makes you ill.
explain: Immunity means your body can recognise and destroy a particular germ quickly. After an infection or a vaccine, memory cells remember the germ, so the next time it arrives the body makes antibodies fast. That is why you rarely get measles twice. An allergy is the opposite kind of problem: the body overreacts to something harmless.

clues: Patients rarely meet this doctor, even though their work guides many diagnoses.
They study blood, urine and tiny pieces of tissue to find out what disease a person has.
Their reports might show which germ is causing an infection, or whether a lump is harmful.
explain: A pathologist is a doctor who works in the lab. They study blood, urine and tissue under a microscope and with other tests to find the cause of disease. Their reports tell other doctors which germ is present or whether cells look healthy. A radiologist reads X-rays and scans instead.

clues: The word comes from the Italian for forty, the number of days ships once had to wait before landing.
People who may have been near an infection are kept apart from others for a while, even if they feel fine.
It is a waiting period that stops a germ passing to new people.
explain: Quarantine keeps people who may have caught a germ away from others until it is clear whether they are ill. It is different from isolation, which keeps people who are already ill apart. Because some germs spread before symptoms appear, quarantine can stop an outbreak growing.

scenario: A 4-year-old swallowed a small coin an hour ago. She is breathing normally and not in pain. The doctor wants to see exactly where the coin is now. Which test is best?
optionNotes: Metal shows up clearly as white
Checks kidneys and infection, not position
explain: Metal blocks X-rays, so a coin shows up as a bright white circle on the picture. The doctor can see whether it is in the food pipe or has reached the stomach. Most small coins in the stomach pass out naturally, but one stuck in the food pipe needs to be removed. A swallowed button battery is more dangerous and needs urgent care.

scenario: Ravi lives near a pond with many mosquitoes. For a week he has had bouts of high fever with shivering, which come and go every couple of days and end with heavy sweating. Which disease is most likely?
optionNotes: Steady rising fever from dirty food
Repeated fever and chills from mosquitoes
explain: The malaria parasite multiplies inside red blood cells and bursts out in cycles. Each burst causes a bout of shivering, high fever and then sweating, often every two or three days. A blood test confirms it, and the right medicines cure it. Mosquito nets and removing standing water help prevent it.

scenario: During the monsoon, a girl has a high fever, severe body ache and pain behind her eyes. Her blood test shows her platelet count is falling. Which disease is most likely?
optionNotes: High fever, eye pain, low platelets
explain: Dengue is a virus spread by Aedes mosquitoes, which breed in standing water after rain. It causes high fever, strong body aches and pain behind the eyes. It can lower platelets, the blood cells that help stop bleeding, so doctors check them with repeated blood tests and keep the patient well hydrated.

scenario: A man has coughed for over three weeks, sweats at night and has lost weight. The doctor wants to look for the bacteria that cause tuberculosis. Which sample should the lab test?
optionNotes: Used for kidney and bladder infections
Coughed up from deep in the lungs
explain: TB of the lungs causes a long cough, night sweats and weight loss. The bacteria live deep in the lungs, so the patient coughs up phlegm, also called sputum, and the lab looks for the bacteria in it. A chest X-ray is often done too. In India, TB testing and treatment are free at government centres.

scenario: A 7-year-old has a mild fever and an itchy rash of small fluid-filled blisters on her chest, face and back. Two classmates had the same rash last week. Which disease is most likely?
optionNotes: Single ring-shaped patch, from a fungus
Red skin only where sun reached
Flat red rash, no fluid blisters
Itchy fluid blisters, spreads in class
explain: Chickenpox is caused by a virus that spreads very easily. It starts with a mild fever, then itchy, fluid-filled blisters appear in crops and crust over in about a week. The child should stay home until all blisters have crusted, and avoid scratching to prevent scars and infection.

scenario: After drinking from the same well, several villagers have sudden, very watery diarrhoea and are getting weak. While they are taken to a doctor, what is the most important first step?
options: Stop all drinks until the diarrhoea ends
Give ORS (oral rehydration solution) to drink
answer: Give ORS (oral rehydration solution) to drink
explain: Sudden watery diarrhoea in many people who share a water source suggests cholera. The real danger is losing too much water and salt. ORS, a mix of clean water, salt and sugar, is absorbed by the gut even during diarrhoea and replaces what is lost. Doctors may also give antibiotics, and the well must be checked and cleaned.

scenario: A girl has flu, with fever, body aches and a cough. Her parent asks the doctor for antibiotics to cure it fast. What is the best advice?
options: Take leftover antibiotics from last year
Take a double dose of antibiotics
Antibiotics do not work on flu; rest and drink fluids
Any antibiotic will cure it in a day
answer: Antibiotics do not work on flu; rest and drink fluids
optionNotes: Harmful and does nothing to a virus
Flu is a virus; the body clears it
explain: Flu is caused by a virus. Antibiotics only work on bacteria, so they will not help and may cause side effects and antibiotic resistance. Rest, fluids and the doctor's advice help the body clear the virus in about a week. A yearly flu vaccine lowers the chance of catching it.

scenario: A boy steps on a nail in a muddy field. The wound is cleaned well. His last tetanus shot was over ten years ago. What should the doctor give to protect him?
optionNotes: Nothing to do with the wound
explain: Tetanus bacteria live in soil and dust and can enter through deep or dirty wounds; the rust on a nail is not the cause. Their poison makes muscles lock tight. Protection from the tetanus vaccine fades over time, so a booster dose is needed after some years, and sooner after a dirty wound.

scenario: A teenager says her heart sometimes feels like it is fluttering or skipping beats. The doctor wants to record the heart's electrical signals using small stickers on her chest. Which test is this?
explain: Each heartbeat is started by a tiny electrical signal. An ECG (electrocardiogram) picks up these signals through stickers on the skin and draws them as a wavy line. Doctors read the pattern to see if the heart's rhythm is normal. The test is quick and painless.

scenario: A girl feels a burning pain when she pees and needs to go very often. She also has a mild fever. The doctor suspects germs in her urine. Which test should come first?
optionNotes: Looks for germs and white cells in urine
explain: Burning and needing to pee often are common signs of a urinary infection, usually caused by bacteria. A urine test checks for germs and for white blood cells, which gather where there is infection. If bacteria are found, the doctor prescribes the right antibiotic. Drinking enough water helps flush germs out.

scenario: A girl has had bad headaches for months. Her doctor wants a very detailed picture of the soft tissue inside her head, without using X-rays. Which test should be ordered?
explain: An MRI scan uses a strong magnet and radio waves to make very detailed pictures of soft tissues like the brain. It uses no X-rays. The patient lies still inside a tube for some minutes while the machine knocks loudly. Most headaches have simple causes, but MRI helps doctors rule out other problems.

scenario: Grandma says her vision has become cloudy and blurry, like looking through a foggy window. The family doctor refers her to a specialist. Which doctor should she see?
explain: General physicians treat common problems and send patients to specialists when needed. An ophthalmologist is an eye doctor who can examine the eye closely and do eye surgery. Cloudy vision in older people is often caused by a cataract, a clouding of the eye's lens, which can be fixed with a short operation.

scenario: A baby gets her measles vaccine. Her older brother asks how a shot today can stop measles years later. What is the best answer?
options: It teaches her immune system to recognise measles and remember it
It kills every germ in her body forever
It is a vitamin that makes her stronger
It only works after she catches measles
answer: It teaches her immune system to recognise measles and remember it
optionNotes: Memory cells stay ready for years
Vaccines target one germ, not all
explain: The vaccine contains a weakened measles virus that cannot cause the real illness. Her immune system makes antibodies and memory cells against it. If real measles ever enters her body, the memory cells recognise it and respond fast. That is why the vaccine protects for many years.

scenario: A newborn is too young for some vaccines. The doctor asks the parents, grandparents and older siblings to make sure their own vaccines are up to date. Why?
options: Their vaccines travel to the baby through the air
Vaccinated family members are less likely to catch germs and pass them to the baby
It makes the baby's blood stronger
Only vaccinated people may legally hold babies
answer: Vaccinated family members are less likely to catch germs and pass them to the baby
optionNotes: Vaccines do not pass through air
Protects the baby by blocking spread
Family vaccines do not change baby's blood
explain: A newborn's immune system is still learning. If the people around the baby are vaccinated, germs have a much harder time reaching the baby. When enough people in a community are vaccinated, a germ cannot spread easily, which also protects those who cannot be vaccinated. This is called herd immunity.

scenario: After eating cut fruit from a roadside stall, a boy's fever rises slowly, day by day, over a week. He has stomach pain and feels very weak. A blood culture grows bacteria. Which disease is most likely?
optionNotes: Bacteria from dirty food; slowly rising fever
