explain: Typhoid is caused by bacteria that spread through food or water dirtied with germs. Its fever typically climbs step by step over several days, with stomach pain and weakness. A blood culture, where blood is kept warm in the lab so any bacteria can grow, confirms it, and antibiotics treat it. A typhoid vaccine and safe food and water help prevent it.

scenario: A blood test shows a child has many more white blood cells than normal. She also has a fever and a painful ear. What does the high white cell count most likely suggest?
options: Her body is fighting an infection
She has been sleeping too much
answer: Her body is fighting an infection
optionNotes: White cells multiply to fight germs
Shown by an X-ray, not white cells
explain: When germs invade, the bone marrow makes and releases more white blood cells to fight them. A complete blood count counts the different blood cells, so a high white cell number, together with fever and ear pain, points to an infection such as an ear infection. The doctor then decides on treatment.

notes: Carries blood away from the heart
Carries blood back to the heart
Carries air down to the lungs
Tiny tube where blood swaps materials
reason: The windpipe carries air; the other four are blood vessels.
explain: Blood travels around your body inside tubes called blood vessels. Arteries (like the aorta) carry blood away from the heart, veins bring it back, and tiny capillaries connect the two. The windpipe is also a tube, but it belongs to the breathing system and carries air, not blood.
fact: An adult body holds about 5 litres of blood.

notes: Green juice from the liver for digestion
Help blood clot at a cut
reason: Bile is a digestive juice; the other four are parts of blood.
explain: Blood has four main parts. Plasma is the liquid that everything floats in, red cells carry oxygen, white cells fight germs, and platelets help seal cuts. Bile is made by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It helps break down fat in your food, so it belongs to digestion, not blood.

notes: Top-left room; receives blood from lungs
Top-right room; receives blood from body
Bottom-right room; pumps blood to lungs
Bottom-left room; pumps blood to body
reason: The aorta is a blood vessel; the other four are the heart's chambers.
explain: Your heart has four hollow rooms called chambers. The two on top, the atria, collect blood coming in. The two at the bottom, the ventricles, squeeze hard to push blood out. The aorta is not a chamber. It is the large tube that carries blood out of the left ventricle to the rest of the body.

notes: Takes blood from heart to body
Takes blood from heart to lungs
Takes blood up the neck to the brain
reason: The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood; the other four carry oxygen-rich blood.
explain: Most arteries carry blood full of oxygen. The pulmonary artery is the exception. It takes used, oxygen-poor blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs, where the blood picks up fresh oxygen. So the rule is that arteries always carry blood away from the heart, whether or not that blood is rich in oxygen.
fact: 'Pulmonary' comes from the Latin word for lung.

notes: Less red colour in the blood
Body struggles to get enough oxygen
Clears dust or germs from the nose
reason: Sneezing is not a sign of anaemia; the other four are.
explain: Anaemia means the blood has too little haemoglobin, the red substance that carries oxygen. With less oxygen reaching the muscles and brain, a person feels tired, dizzy and out of breath, and their skin can look pale. Sneezing is the nose clearing dust or germs and has nothing to do with anaemia.

notes: Sits at the centre of haemoglobin
Needed to build healthy red cells
A B-vitamin needed to make red cells
reason: Vitamin K helps blood clot; the other four are needed to make red blood cells.
explain: Your bone marrow makes millions of new red blood cells every second, and it needs raw materials. Iron and protein build haemoglobin, while vitamin B12 and folic acid help the cells grow and divide properly. Vitamin K has a different job: the liver uses it to make clotting proteins that stop bleeding.

notes: Cell pieces that plug a wound
Net that traps cells at a cut
Dried clot that protects healing skin
reason: Haemoglobin carries oxygen; the other four are part of clotting.
explain: When you cut yourself, platelets rush in and stick together to plug the hole. Clotting factors in the plasma then make long fibrin threads that form a net, trapping blood cells into a clot. The clot dries into a scab while new skin grows underneath. Haemoglobin plays no part in this; its job is carrying oxygen.

notes: Artery runs close to the skin here
No large artery to press on
Artery used when measuring blood pressure
Small artery over the foot bones
reason: You cannot feel a pulse at the tip of the nose; you can at the other four places.
explain: A pulse is the throb of an artery stretching each time the heart pushes blood into it. You can feel it wherever a fairly large artery runs close to the skin over something firm, like a bone. The wrist, neck, inner elbow and top of the foot all have such arteries. The tip of the nose has only tiny vessels, so there is no pulse to feel.

notes: Body is resting, needs less oxygen
reason: Deep sleep slows the heart; the other four speed it up.
explain: Your heart speeds up whenever your body needs more oxygen delivered quickly. Exercise makes muscles hungry for oxygen, fear releases a hormone called adrenaline, and a fever makes the body's chemistry run faster. In deep sleep your body needs the least energy, so your heart rate drops.

notes: Has a nucleus; contracts to move you
Has a nucleus; covers the body
reason: A mature human red blood cell has no nucleus; the others do.
explain: The nucleus is the control centre of a cell and holds its DNA. As a human red blood cell matures in the bone marrow, it pushes its nucleus out. That leaves more space for haemoglobin, so each cell carries more oxygen. Without a nucleus it cannot repair itself, which is why a red cell lives only about four months.
fact: A red blood cell lives for about 120 days before it is recycled.

notes: Body holds extra water, raising pressure
Heart must push blood through more tissue
Keeps blood vessels healthy and flexible
reason: Daily exercise helps keep blood pressure healthy; the other four raise it.
explain: Blood pressure is how hard blood pushes on the walls of your arteries. Salt makes the body hold extra water, so there is more blood to push. Smoking stiffens vessel walls, and extra body weight and long-term stress make the heart work harder. Regular exercise strengthens the heart and keeps arteries flexible, which helps keep pressure normal.

notes: Valve between right atrium and ventricle
Muscle wall between left and right sides
Valve between left atrium and ventricle
Valve where blood leaves for the body
Valve where blood leaves for the lungs
reason: The septum is a wall; the other four are the heart's valves.
explain: The heart has four valves that act like one-way doors, so blood can only move forward. The tricuspid and mitral valves sit between the upper and lower chambers. The aortic and pulmonary valves sit where blood leaves the heart. The septum is a thick wall of muscle that keeps the left and right sides of the heart apart.

notes: Carried by red cells from lungs
Passes through the gut, never enters blood
Waste gas carried to the lungs
reason: Fibre is never absorbed into the blood; the other four are carried in it.
explain: Blood is the body's delivery service. It carries oxygen from the lungs, sugar from digested food, and hormones from glands to the cells, and takes waste like carbon dioxide away. Fibre from fruits, vegetables and grains is not absorbed at all. It stays in the gut and helps waste move along.

notes: Sound-wave video of the beating heart
Measures how much air you blow out
reason: A spirometer tests the lungs; the other four check the heart and blood vessels.
explain: A heart doctor has several ways to check the heart. A stethoscope lets them hear the valves closing, a cuff measures blood pressure, an ECG records the tiny electrical signals that trigger each beat, and an echocardiogram uses sound waves to show the heart moving. A spirometer measures how much air you can breathe out, so it is a lung test.

reason: A frog's heart has three chambers; the other four animals have four.
explain: A four-chambered heart keeps oxygen-rich blood on the left side and oxygen-poor blood on the right side, so they never mix. Mammals, birds and crocodiles have this design. A frog's heart has two atria but only one ventricle, so some mixing happens. Frogs manage because they also take in oxygen through their moist skin.
fact: A fish heart has just two chambers.

notes: True of veins, especially in legs
True of veins, close to the skin
reason: Thick muscular walls describe arteries; the other four describe veins.
explain: Arteries take the full force of each heartbeat, so they need thick, muscular, stretchy walls. By the time blood reaches the veins, the pressure is low, so vein walls are thinner. To stop blood slipping backwards, veins have valves. Many veins lie near the skin, which is why nurses use them to take blood samples.

notes: Large white cell that cleans up
reason: A platelet is a clotting fragment; the other four are types of white blood cell.
explain: There are several kinds of white blood cells, each with its own way of fighting germs. Neutrophils swallow bacteria, lymphocytes make antibodies, monocytes clean up dead cells and germs, and eosinophils fight parasites. A platelet is not a full cell at all. It is a small piece broken off a bigger cell, and its job is to help blood clot.

clues: This fist-sized organ works every second of your life, even while you sleep.
It has four rooms inside and squeezes to push blood around your body.
A doctor listens to its 'lub-dub' sound with a stethoscope.
explain: The heart is a muscle about the size of your fist that sits in the middle of your chest, tilted a little to the left. Each time it squeezes, it pushes blood through tubes to every part of your body, delivering oxygen and food to cells. The 'lub-dub' sound comes from its valves snapping shut.
fact: An adult's heart beats about 100,000 times a day.

clues: Its walls are thick, stretchy and muscular, so it can handle high pressure.
When you press on one at your wrist, you can feel a steady throb.
This kind of tube carries red liquid away from the main pumping organ out to the body.
explain: Arteries are the tubes that carry blood away from the heart. The heart pushes blood into them with force, so they have thick, muscular, stretchy walls. The throb you feel at your wrist or neck is an artery stretching each time the heart squeezes.

clues: Tiny flaps inside work like one-way doors, so nothing slides backwards.
These thin-walled tubes carry used, oxygen-poor red liquid back to the chest.
A nurse often puts a needle into one on the inside of your elbow to take a sample.
explain: Veins carry blood back to the heart after it has dropped off its oxygen. The pressure inside them is low, so their walls are thinner than artery walls. Valves inside stop blood from flowing backwards, which matters most in your legs, where blood has to travel upwards.
fact: Veins look bluish through your skin, but the blood inside is dark red. Your skin changes how light reaches your eyes.

clues: These are the narrowest tubes in your circulation; red cells pass through in single file.
Their walls are only one cell thick, so oxygen and food slip through to nearby cells.
They form a net that links the smallest arteries to the smallest veins.
explain: Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels, finer than a hair. Their walls are just one cell thick, so oxygen and nutrients can pass out into the body's cells, and waste can pass in. Every cell in your body is close to a capillary. They are where the real delivery work of the blood happens.

clues: These are not whole cells but small pieces broken off bigger cells in the bone marrow.
At a wound, they become sticky and clump together like a plug.
They help stop the bleeding after you scrape your knee.
explain: Platelets are tiny cell fragments that float in your blood. When a vessel is damaged, they stick to the edges and to each other, forming a plug. They also release chemicals that help build a net of fibrin threads, which traps red cells into a clot. The clot later dries into a scab.

clues: It makes up a little more than half of what flows in your arteries and veins.
It carries dissolved sugar, salts, hormones and waste around the body.
When a sample is spun fast in a machine, it is the pale, straw-coloured layer on top.
explain: Plasma is the liquid part of blood, and it is mostly water. Red cells, white cells and platelets float in it, along with dissolved food, salts, hormones and wastes. When blood is spun in a machine, the heavy cells sink and the pale plasma stays on top.

clues: Without enough of it, a person may feel tired and look pale.
It is packed inside certain cells and gives them their colour.
It grabs a gas in the lungs and lets go of it in the muscles.
explain: Haemoglobin is a protein packed inside red blood cells. Each molecule has iron at its centre, which grabs oxygen in the lungs and releases it where cells need it. Haemoglobin is what makes blood red. When there is too little of it, a person has anaemia.

clues: A doctor counts it for 15 seconds and multiplies by four.
It gets faster when you run and slower when you rest.
You feel it as a gentle throb when you press two fingers just below the thumb side of your palm.
explain: Your pulse is the throb you feel each time your heart pushes a wave of blood through your arteries. Counting it tells you how many times your heart beats in a minute. For a resting child it is usually somewhere around 70 to 110, and it rises with exercise, excitement or fever.

clues: It can stay too high for years without any warning signs, so adults should get it checked.
It is written as two numbers, such as 120 over 80.
A band wrapped round your upper arm fills with air to measure it.
explain: Blood pressure is how hard blood presses on the walls of your arteries. The top number is the pressure while the heart squeezes, and the bottom number is the pressure while it relaxes between beats. If it stays high for a long time, it strains the heart and blood vessels, so doctors check it regularly in adults.

clues: Many girls and women in India have this condition.
It means there is not enough haemoglobin to carry oxygen around the body.
People with it feel weak and breathless on stairs; spinach, lentils and eggs can help.
explain: Anaemia means the blood has too little haemoglobin, so less oxygen reaches the body's cells. The most common cause is not getting enough iron, which the body needs to make haemoglobin. Girls and women need more iron because they lose some blood each month during periods. Iron-rich foods, and iron tablets when a doctor prescribes them, help.

clues: Veins in your legs have them too, so blood does not slide back down.
They make sure blood moves only one way through the heart.
The heart has four of them, and their snapping shut makes the 'lub-dub' sound.
explain: A valve is a set of thin flaps that lets blood pass in one direction and then shuts to stop it flowing back. The heart has four valves. A doctor can hear them through a stethoscope: 'lub' is the sound of two valves shutting, and 'dub' is the other two.

clues: The one on the left has the thickest, strongest muscle wall in the heart.
The heart has two of these, one on each side, below the two collecting rooms.
They squeeze hard to push blood out into the arteries.
explain: The ventricles are the two lower chambers of the heart and do the hard pushing. The right ventricle sends blood a short distance to the lungs. The left ventricle sends blood all the way to your head and toes, so its wall is much thicker and stronger.

clues: It curves over like the handle of a walking stick, then runs down through the chest and belly.
Every drop of oxygen-rich blood leaving the left ventricle passes through it first.
It is the largest of the tubes that carry blood away from the chest's main pumping organ.
explain: The aorta is the body's main artery. It leaves the left ventricle, curves over the top of the heart, and runs down in front of the backbone. Smaller arteries branch off it to carry oxygen-rich blood to the head, arms, organs and legs. In an adult it is about as wide as a garden hose.

clues: Its name comes from a Latin word for an entrance hall.
The heart has two of these, and each one collects blood coming in from veins.
They sit above the two bigger, stronger squeezing rooms of the heart.
explain: The two atria are the upper chambers of the heart. The right one receives oxygen-poor blood from the body, and the left one receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs. Their walls are thin because they only need to push blood a short way down into the ventricles.

clues: Over a week or two it may turn green and then yellow as your body cleans it up.
It forms when tiny tubes break and leak under the surface after a bump.
You might get one on your leg after banging it on a table.
explain: A hard bump can break capillaries under the skin. Blood leaks out and gets trapped, which shows as a dark mark. Over the next days your body breaks down the haemoglobin in that blood into other substances that look green and then yellow, and finally clears it away. A cold pack wrapped in cloth soon after the bump can reduce swelling.

clues: Your bone marrow makes about two million of these every second.
When fully grown they have no nucleus, which leaves more room for their cargo.
Shaped like a doughnut without a hole, they carry the gas you breathe in to every cell.
explain: Red blood cells are the most common cells in your blood. They are packed with haemoglobin, which picks up oxygen in the lungs and drops it off around the body. Their dented shape gives them a large surface for taking in oxygen, and they are bendy enough to squeeze through narrow capillaries.
fact: Each red blood cell lives about 120 days.

clues: Healthy adults can do this every few months, and the body soon replaces what was taken.
Camps for it are often held in offices, colleges and community halls.
One person doing this can help save lives after accidents and operations.
explain: In blood donation, a healthy adult lets a trained worker collect a unit of their blood, which is stored in a blood bank. It is later given to patients who have lost blood or cannot make enough. The donor's body replaces the liquid part within a day or two and the red cells over the next few weeks.

scenario: A 13-year-old girl feels tired all the time, gets breathless climbing stairs and looks pale. Her blood test shows low haemoglobin. What is the most likely problem?
optionNotes: Too little haemoglobin to carry oxygen
A virus causing runny nose and sneezing
Usually causes no symptoms at all
explain: Low haemoglobin is the key clue. Haemoglobin carries oxygen, so when there is too little, muscles and the brain get less oxygen. That causes tiredness, breathlessness and pale skin. A doctor will look for the cause, which is often too little iron in the diet.

scenario: Your friend cuts his hand on a paper cutter and it is bleeding steadily. An adult is on the way. What should you do first?
options: Press firmly on it with a clean cloth
Wave it in the air to dry it
answer: Press firmly on it with a clean cloth
optionNotes: Hot water can make bleeding worse
Toothpaste does not stop bleeding and can irritate
Pressure helps platelets form a clot
explain: Firm, steady pressure with a clean cloth squeezes the cut edges together and slows the blood, giving platelets time to build a clot. Raising the hand above the heart also helps. Keep pressing for several minutes without lifting to peek. An adult or doctor should check whether the cut needs stitches.

scenario: A doctor wraps a band around a man's upper arm and fills it with air. She slowly lets the air out while listening with a stethoscope and reads two numbers. What is she measuring?
optionNotes: Checked with a clip on the finger
Checked with an inflatable arm cuff
explain: The inflated cuff squeezes the main arm artery shut. As the air is let out, blood starts to push through again, and the doctor hears it. The pressure when the sound starts is the top number (while the heart squeezes). The pressure when it stops is the bottom number (while the heart rests).

scenario: After a road accident, a patient has lost a lot of blood and needs red blood cells immediately. There is no time to test his blood group. Which group of red cells is safest to give?
optionNotes: Has A, B and Rh markers; many people react
Has A and Rh markers; many people react
Has the B marker; many people react
No A, B or Rh markers; safest for anyone
explain: Blood groups depend on markers on the surface of red cells. If a patient receives cells with markers their body does not recognise, their immune system attacks them. O negative red cells have no A, B or Rh markers, so they are the safest choice when there is no time to test. Doctors still check the patient's group as soon as they can.
fact: People with O negative blood are often called universal red cell donors.

scenario: A nurse counts 20 pulse beats at a resting boy's wrist in 15 seconds. What is his pulse rate per minute?
explain: A minute has four lots of 15 seconds, so you multiply the count by four: 20 x 4 = 80. That is a normal resting pulse for a child. Counting for a short time and multiplying is quicker, but counting for a full minute is more accurate if the beat is uneven.

scenario: A girl's nose starts bleeding during class. She is not hurt anywhere else. What is the right first aid while the teacher is told?
options: Sit her up, lean forward, pinch soft part of nose
Tilt her head back and wait
Lie her flat on her back
answer: Sit her up, lean forward, pinch soft part of nose
optionNotes: Pressure stops the leak; blood drains out, not down
Blood runs down the throat and is swallowed
Can injure the inside of the nose
explain: Most nosebleeds come from tiny blood vessels near the front of the nose. Pinching the soft part presses on them so a clot can form, and leaning forward lets blood drip out instead of running down the throat. Pinch for about 10 minutes without letting go. If bleeding does not stop after 20 minutes, or followed a hard knock, an adult should get medical help.

scenario: A doctor hears an extra whooshing sound in a baby's chest. A scan shows a small hole in the muscle wall that separates the left side of the heart from the right side. Which part has the hole?
optionNotes: Muscle wall between left and right sides
Tiny blood vessel in body tissues
explain: The septum keeps oxygen-rich blood on the left side of the heart apart from oxygen-poor blood on the right. Some babies are born with a small hole in it, often called a 'hole in the heart'. Blood leaking through the hole makes the whooshing sound, called a murmur. Many small holes close on their own; larger ones can be repaired by doctors.

scenario: A man gets chest pain when he walks fast, and it goes away when he rests. Tests show that the arteries supplying his heart muscle with blood have become narrow. Which arteries are these?
optionNotes: Bring blood from the lungs into the heart
Wrap around and feed the heart muscle
Bring used blood back into the heart
Carry blood up the neck to the brain
explain: The heart muscle needs its own oxygen supply, and it gets it from the coronary arteries that wrap around its surface like a crown. If fatty deposits narrow them, the heart muscle gets too little oxygen when it works hard, which causes chest pain. Healthy food, regular exercise and not smoking help keep these arteries open.
fact: 'Coronary' comes from the Latin word for crown.

scenario: A girl bruises very easily and has tiny red spots on her skin. Her blood test shows that the part of her blood that plugs leaks in vessels is very low. Which part is it?
optionNotes: Carry oxygen; low count causes tiredness
Clump together to seal leaking vessels
explain: Tiny vessels in the body get small leaks all the time, and platelets seal them before we notice. When platelets are low, blood escapes under the skin easily, causing bruises and pinpoint red spots. A pathologist counts platelets with a blood test, and a doctor then looks for the reason they are low.

scenario: A 50-year-old man has high blood pressure. He eats pickles, papads and salty snacks every day. Along with his doctor's treatment, which change will help his blood pressure most?
optionNotes: Can cause dehydration; does not fix pressure
Less salt means less water held in blood
Poor sleep can raise blood pressure
Skipping meals does not lower pressure
explain: Salt makes the body hold on to extra water, which increases the amount of blood in the vessels and raises the pressure. Pickles, papads and packaged snacks contain a lot of salt. Cutting down on them, along with exercise and any medicine the doctor prescribes, helps bring blood pressure down.

scenario: A teenager has anaemia because her body is short of a mineral needed to make haemoglobin. Her nutritionist suggests more green leafy vegetables, lentils and eggs. Which mineral is it?
optionNotes: Found in salt; controls water balance
Sits at the centre of haemoglobin
explain: Every haemoglobin molecule needs iron to hold on to oxygen. Without enough iron, the body makes fewer and paler red blood cells, and the person has anaemia. Leafy greens, lentils, beans and eggs supply iron. Eating them with vitamin C foods like amla, lemon or guava helps the body absorb more of it.

scenario: A shopkeeper who stands all day has swollen, twisted, bluish tubes on the backs of his legs. The one-way flaps inside them have become weak, so blood collects there. Which blood vessels are these?
optionNotes: Too tiny to see bulging like this
explain: Blood in the leg veins has to travel upwards against gravity. Valves inside the veins stop it from sliding back down, and leg muscles squeeze the veins to help. If the valves weaken, blood pools and the veins swell and twist; these are called varicose veins. Walking, raising the legs and not standing still for hours all help.

scenario: During a long school assembly in the heat, a boy says he feels dizzy and then slumps to the floor. He is breathing normally. What should the teacher do first?
options: Lay him on his back and raise his legs
answer: Lay him on his back and raise his legs
optionNotes: Standing can make him faint again
Helps blood flow back to the brain
Food will not help him wake up
Can shock him; does not help blood flow
explain: Standing still for a long time, especially in heat, lets blood pool in the legs. Less blood reaches the brain, and the person faints. Lying flat with the legs raised helps blood return to the heart and brain, and most people wake within a minute. If he does not wake up quickly, the teacher should call for emergency help.

scenario: A student asks which heart chamber pushes oxygen-rich blood out to the whole body, from head to toes. It has the thickest muscle wall of all four. Which chamber is it?
optionNotes: Collects used blood from the body
Collects fresh blood from the lungs
Pushes blood only to the nearby lungs
Pushes blood to the whole body
explain: The left ventricle receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and sends it into the aorta. Because that blood has to reach every part of the body, the left ventricle needs the most force, so its wall is the thickest. The right ventricle only sends blood to the lungs next door, so its wall is thinner.

scenario: A woman donated blood last week. Her body is now making new red blood cells to replace the ones she gave. Where in her body are these new cells made?
optionNotes: Soft tissue inside bones; the blood-cell factory
Pushes blood around; makes no cells
explain: Bone marrow is the soft, spongy tissue inside bones such as the hips, ribs and breastbone. It makes red cells, white cells and platelets. After a donation, a hormone from the kidneys tells the marrow to speed up, and the red cells are fully replaced over the next several weeks.

scenario: A child's red blood cells look stiff and curved like a crescent moon. They get stuck in small vessels and break down early, making the child tired. The condition runs in families. What is it?
optionNotes: Cells are small and pale, not curved
Inherited, but blood does not clot well
Inherited; red cells bend into crescents
Not caused by misshaped red cells
explain: Sickle cell disease is passed from parents to children through genes. It changes haemoglobin so that red cells turn stiff and crescent-shaped. These cells block small vessels, causing pain, and they break down quickly, causing anaemia. It cannot be caught from someone, and treatment helps people with it lead active lives.
fact: India runs a national mission to screen for and reduce sickle cell disease.

notes: Gland in the front of the neck
Sends spit into the mouth through tubes
Sits on top of each kidney
Tiny gland deep in the brain
reason: Salivary glands pour saliva through tubes into the mouth; the others release hormones straight into the blood.
explain: Glands are body parts that make and release useful substances. Endocrine glands have no tubes (ducts); they release hormones straight into the blood, which carries them all over the body. Salivary glands are different: they send saliva through tiny tubes into your mouth to start digesting food.
fact: The pituitary gland is only about the size of a pea, yet it controls several other glands.

notes: Prepares the body for sudden danger
Sets how fast the body uses energy
Helps bones and muscles get bigger
reason: Haemoglobin is an oxygen-carrying protein inside red blood cells; the others are hormones.
explain: Hormones are chemical messengers. A gland makes them, the blood carries them, and they tell other parts of the body what to do. Haemoglobin is not a messenger: it is the red protein inside red blood cells that picks up oxygen in the lungs and drops it off around the body.

notes: Where a baby grows before birth
reason: The bladder belongs to the excretory system; the rest are reproductive organs.
explain: The reproductive system is the set of organs that lets living things make babies. In females, the ovaries make eggs and the uterus is where a baby develops. In males, the testes make sperm and the sperm ducts carry them. The bladder only stores urine until you go to the toilet, so it belongs to the excretory system.

reason: First teeth come in during babyhood; the others are changes of puberty.
explain: Puberty is the stage, usually starting between about 8 and 14 years of age, when a child's body begins changing into an adult's. Sex hormones from the ovaries or testes cause growth spurts, oilier skin, new body hair and, especially in boys, a deeper voice. A baby's first teeth come in between about 6 months and 3 years, long before puberty.

notes: Hormone that moves sugar into cells
reason: Iodine is linked to the thyroid; the other four are all part of the diabetes story.
explain: Diabetes is a condition where there is too much sugar in the blood. It happens when the pancreas makes too little insulin, or when the body stops responding to insulin properly. People with diabetes check their sugar level with a small glucose meter. Iodine is not part of this; the thyroid gland uses it to make its hormone.

reason: The pancreas controls blood sugar; the other four are all connected to the thyroid gland.
explain: The thyroid gland in your neck makes thyroxine, a hormone that controls how fast your body uses energy. It needs iodine from food to make it. When food has too little iodine, the thyroid can grow larger and form a lump called a goitre. Adding iodine to salt has made goitre much less common. The pancreas is a different gland that controls blood sugar.

notes: Lets more light into the eyes
reason: Adrenaline makes you alert; the other four are its effects.
explain: When you get a fright, your adrenal glands release adrenaline within seconds. It prepares the body to fight or run away: the heart beats faster, breathing speeds up, the pupils widen and extra blood flows to the muscles. Feeling sleepy is the opposite, because adrenaline makes you more alert.
fact: The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys like small caps.

notes: Sugar and gas, no building nutrients
reason: Fizzy drinks do not help growth; the other four do.
explain: Children grow when growth hormone from the pituitary gland tells bones and muscles to get bigger. Much of it is released during deep sleep, so good sleep matters. The body also needs protein and minerals as building materials, and exercise makes bones stronger. Fizzy drinks give sugar but none of the building blocks for growth.
fact: A large share of your daily growth hormone is released in the first few hours of deep sleep at night.

notes: Monthly cycle that starts in girls
Hair on chin and upper lip
Bump at the front of the neck
reason: Periods happen only in girls; the other four are puberty changes in boys.
explain: At puberty, a boy's testes make more testosterone. This hormone makes the voice box grow (seen as the Adam's apple), the voice deepen, facial hair appear and the shoulders widen. In girls, the ovaries make oestrogen, which leads to periods, also called menstruation. A period is a normal monthly cycle in which the lining of the uterus is shed.

reason: The thyroid makes thyroxine, not adrenaline; the other four pairs are correct.
explain: Each endocrine gland makes its own hormones. The pancreas makes insulin, the adrenal glands make adrenaline, the pituitary makes growth hormone and the testes make testosterone. The thyroid gland makes thyroxine, which controls how fast the body uses energy, so pairing it with adrenaline is wrong.

notes: Body tries to replace lost water
Caused by dust, pollen or colds
reason: Sneezing is not a sign of diabetes; the other four are.
explain: In diabetes, sugar builds up in the blood instead of entering the cells. The kidneys try to flush the extra sugar out, so the person pees a lot and feels very thirsty. The cells are short of fuel, so the person feels tired, and high sugar also slows healing. Sneezing comes from things like dust, pollen or a cold, not from diabetes.

reason: A dog does not go through metamorphosis; the other four do.
explain: Metamorphosis is a big change in body shape as a young animal becomes an adult. Hormones control it: in frogs, thyroxine from the thyroid turns a tadpole into a frog, and insects use hormones of their own. A puppy simply grows bigger; its body plan stays the same.
fact: Without enough thyroxine, a tadpole cannot change into a frog.

notes: Works when the pituitary signals it
reason: The pancreas responds directly to blood sugar; the other four are switched on by pituitary hormones.
explain: The pituitary is called the master gland because it sends out hormones that switch other glands on, such as the thyroid, adrenal glands, ovaries and testes. The pancreas works differently. Its hormone-making cells sense the sugar level in the blood directly and release insulin or glucagon as needed.

reason: Popping pimples harms the skin; the other four are healthy habits during puberty.
explain: During puberty, sweat and oil glands become more active, so a daily bath and clean clothes keep body odour and germs down. A balanced diet, enough sleep and exercise support the growth spurt. Popping pimples pushes germs deeper into the skin and can leave scars, so it is better to wash gently and leave them alone.

notes: Tells the liver to release stored sugar
reason: Insulin lowers blood sugar; the other four raise it.
explain: The body keeps blood sugar in a safe range using hormones that push in opposite directions. Several hormones, including glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol, raise blood sugar, for example by telling the liver to release the sugar it has stored. Insulin is the main hormone that lowers blood sugar, by helping cells take sugar in.

notes: Shows if sugar is too high or low
Insulin or tablets the doctor advises
reason: Eating lots of sweets raises blood sugar; the other four are part of good diabetes care.
explain: People with diabetes keep their blood sugar steady by eating balanced meals, being active and checking their sugar level often. Many also take insulin or other medicines exactly as their doctor tells them. Eating lots of sweets makes blood sugar shoot up, which is the problem diabetes care tries to prevent.

reason: Bile comes from the liver; the pancreas makes the other four.
explain: The pancreas has two jobs. As an endocrine gland, it releases insulin and glucagon into the blood to control sugar. As a digestive gland, it sends enzymes such as trypsin and lipase into the small intestine through a duct. Bile is made by the liver, not the pancreas, and helps break fat into tiny droplets.

clues: Tiny amounts of this can change how you grow, sleep or react to a fright.
It is made in one place and travels around the body to give orders to far-away organs.
Insulin, adrenaline and thyroxine are all examples.
explain: A hormone is a chemical messenger. An endocrine gland releases it into the blood, the blood carries it everywhere, and only the cells that have the right receivers respond. That is how a gland in your neck or head can control things happening in your bones, skin or heart.

clues: Special cells in a leaf-shaped organ behind the stomach release it after a meal.
It works like a key, letting glucose leave the blood and enter cells.
People whose bodies cannot make it must take it every day to stay healthy.
explain: After you eat, glucose from food enters your blood. The pancreas releases insulin, which lets cells take in that glucose and use it for energy. Without insulin, glucose stays stuck in the blood, which is what happens in type 1 diabetes. Glucagon does the opposite job and raises blood glucose.

clues: Its hormone sets how fast your body burns energy, like a speed dial.
If it works too slowly, a person may feel tired and cold all the time.
This gland sits in front of your windpipe, just below the Adam's apple.
explain: The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck. It makes thyroxine, which controls metabolism, the speed at which your cells use energy. Too little thyroxine makes a person slow, tired and cold; too much makes them shaky, hot and thin.

clues: Its hormones switch on the thyroid, adrenal glands, ovaries and testes.
It hangs from the underside of the head's control centre, just behind the eyes.
It is about the size of a small bean and makes the hormone that helps children get taller.
explain: The pituitary is a pea-sized gland under the brain. It is called the master gland because its hormones control other glands, telling them when to work harder or slow down. It also makes growth hormone, which helps children's bones and muscles get bigger.

clues: Doctors may use an injection of it to treat a severe allergic reaction.
It makes your heart race and your palms sweat when you are scared or excited.
It is made by small glands that sit on top of the organs that make urine.
explain: Adrenaline is the emergency hormone, made by the adrenal glands on top of the kidneys. In seconds it raises your heart rate, speeds up breathing and sends extra blood and sugar to your muscles, so you can fight or run. Because it opens airways and supports blood pressure, doctors also use it in emergencies such as a severe allergic reaction.

clues: It usually begins somewhere between about 8 and 14 years of age.
During this time, voices may deepen, pimples may appear and new hair grows in the armpits.
It is the stage when a child's body slowly changes into a grown-up's body.
explain: Puberty is when the body becomes able to have children one day. The pituitary gland signals the ovaries or testes to make sex hormones, and these cause the changes: growth spurts, body hair, oilier skin, breast development in girls and a deeper voice in boys. It starts at different ages for different people, and that is normal.

clues: Doctors check for it by measuring glucose in a blood sample.
People with it may feel very thirsty and need to pee often.
With it, the body cannot control glucose in the blood, so the level gets too high.
explain: In diabetes, the body either makes too little insulin (type 1) or does not respond to it well (type 2). Glucose then stays in the blood instead of feeding the cells. Over time, high blood glucose can harm the eyes, kidneys and nerves, so people with diabetes manage it with diet, exercise, regular checks and medicine.

clues: It used to be very common in hilly areas far from the sea.
Adding a special mineral to table salt has made it much rarer.
It is a visible lump at the front of the throat, caused by an enlarged gland.
explain: The thyroid gland needs iodine to make its hormone. When food has too little iodine, the gland grows larger as it tries to make enough, forming a goitre. Soil in hilly regions often has little iodine, which is why goitre was common there. Iodised salt is a simple way to prevent it.

clues: Girls' bodies also make a small amount of it.
At puberty it makes the voice box grow, so the voice gets deeper.
It is the main sex hormone made in the organs that produce sperm.
explain: Testosterone is made mainly by the testes. At puberty it causes the changes seen in boys: deeper voice, facial and body hair, more muscle and broader shoulders. It also helps the testes make sperm. Girls make small amounts too, but their main sex hormone is oestrogen.

clues: Together with another hormone, it helps prepare the lining of the uterus each month.
At puberty it causes breasts to develop and hips to widen.
It is the main sex hormone made by the organs that release eggs.
explain: Oestrogen (also spelled estrogen) is made mainly by the ovaries. At puberty it causes the body changes seen in girls, such as breast development and wider hips. Each month it also helps thicken the lining of the uterus, working with another hormone called progesterone.

clues: It usually starts about two years after the first signs of puberty in girls.
It happens roughly every 28 days and lasts a few days each time.
If an egg is not fertilised, the thick lining of the womb breaks down and leaves the body.
explain: Every month, the lining of the uterus thickens so it could hold a baby if an egg were fertilised. When that does not happen, the lining breaks down and flows out of the body for a few days. This is menstruation, or a period. It is a normal, healthy sign that the reproductive system is working.

clues: Its thick muscular wall can stretch to many times its normal size.
Each month its lining thickens, ready in case an egg is fertilised.
It is the hollow, pear-shaped organ where an unborn child develops for about nine months.
explain: The uterus, or womb, is a hollow muscular organ in the female body. If a fertilised egg settles in its lining, the baby grows there for about nine months while the uterus stretches to make room. Its strong muscles also push the baby out at birth. The ovaries, which make eggs, sit on either side of it.

clues: In humans it happens inside the tube that leads from the ovary to the uterus.
In most fish and frogs it happens outside the body, in water.
It is the moment when a male sex cell and a female sex cell fuse to start a new life.
explain: Fertilisation is when a sperm and an egg fuse to form one new cell, called a zygote. In humans it happens inside the body, in the oviduct, so it is called internal fertilisation. Frogs and most fish release eggs and sperm into water, where fertilisation happens outside the body.

clues: This bump is made of tough, bendy cartilage.
It usually becomes easier to see when a teenager's sound box grows during puberty.
It moves up and down when you swallow, and it is named after a fruit.
explain: The Adam's apple is the front edge of the voice box (larynx), which is made of cartilage. At puberty, testosterone makes the voice box grow, especially in boys, so the bump becomes more visible. A bigger voice box has longer vocal cords, which is why the voice gets deeper.

clues: Much of it is released in the first few hours of deep sleep.
If a child makes too little, a doctor may prescribe daily injections of it.
It tells bones and muscles to get bigger during childhood, so a child gains centimetres each year.
explain: Growth hormone is made by the pituitary gland. It tells the ends of long bones to lengthen and muscles to build up, which is how children get taller. Most of it is released during deep sleep, which is one reason growing children need plenty of sleep.

clues: This specialist might treat a child who is growing much more slowly than expected.
They look after patients with thyroid problems or blood glucose problems.
Their speciality is the body's system of ductless organs that release chemical messengers.
explain: An endocrinologist is a doctor who treats problems of the endocrine system, the glands that make hormones. They treat diabetes, thyroid disease, growth problems and puberty that comes very early or very late. A cardiologist treats the heart, a neurologist the brain and nerves, and a nephrologist the kidneys.

clues: Along with body changes, feelings can become stronger and friendships matter more during this stage.
The World Health Organization describes it as roughly ages 10 to 19.
It is the stage of life that bridges childhood and adulthood.
explain: Adolescence is the whole period of change between being a child and being an adult. It includes puberty, the body changes, but also changes in thinking, feelings and independence. Mood swings during adolescence are common, partly because hormone levels are changing.

scenario: A 9-year-old is always thirsty, wakes at night to pee, and has lost weight even though she eats well. The doctor suspects a hormone problem. Which test should come first?
optionNotes: Checks how well the ears work
explain: Thirst, frequent peeing and weight loss are classic signs of diabetes. When cells cannot use glucose, it builds up in the blood, the kidneys pass it out in urine with lots of water, and the body burns fat and muscle for fuel. A blood sugar test measures glucose directly, so it is the quickest way to check.

scenario: A woman from a hilly village has a slowly growing lump at the front of her neck. Her family uses plain salt with no added minerals. Which nutrient is she probably missing?
optionNotes: Needed for healthy gums and healing
explain: The thyroid gland needs iodine to make thyroxine. Without enough, it grows bigger, forming a lump called a goitre. Hilly areas often have soil and water low in iodine, so iodised salt is an easy way to prevent this. A doctor would confirm it with blood tests.

scenario: A 10-year-old is much shorter than his classmates and has grown very little in two years. Tests show a gland at the base of his brain is making too little of one hormone. Which hormone?
optionNotes: Tells bones and muscles to grow
explain: The pituitary gland sits at the base of the brain and makes growth hormone. If it makes too little, a child grows much more slowly than others. Doctors can treat this with regular growth hormone injections, which help the child catch up.

scenario: Before her school speech, Meera's heart pounds, her palms sweat and she breathes fast. A hormone released within seconds causes this. Which glands release it?
explain: Nervousness triggers the adrenal glands, on top of the kidneys, to release adrenaline. It speeds up the heart and breathing and makes you sweat, getting the body ready for action. These feelings are normal and fade once the moment passes; slow, deep breaths can help.

scenario: A 13-year-old has had oily skin and pimples since puberty began. Her face is not swollen or very painful. What is the best advice?
options: Scrub the face hard many times a day
Wash the face gently twice a day
answer: Wash the face gently twice a day
optionNotes: Pushes germs deeper and can scar
Irritates skin and can worsen pimples
Can irritate and burn the skin
Removes extra oil without harming skin
explain: Puberty hormones make the skin's oil glands more active. Oil and dead skin can block pores, and bacteria then cause pimples. Gentle washing twice a day helps. Squeezing or harsh scrubbing damages the skin. If pimples are severe or leave scars, a dermatologist can prescribe treatment.

scenario: A 14-year-old boy's voice keeps cracking, jumping between high and low. He is otherwise healthy. Which body part is growing and causing this?
optionNotes: Shapes words, does not set pitch
Holds the vocal cords that make sound
Push air but do not set pitch
explain: At puberty, testosterone makes the voice box (larynx) and its vocal cords grow longer and thicker. While they are growing, the voice can crack or jump between high and low. Once growth settles, the voice becomes steadily deeper. This is normal and needs no treatment.

scenario: A boy with diabetes took his insulin but skipped lunch. Now he is shaky, sweaty and confused, but awake and able to swallow. While an adult calls for help, what should he be given first?
options: A sugary drink or glucose tablets
answer: A sugary drink or glucose tablets
optionNotes: Has no sugar to raise levels
Low sugar can get worse unnoticed
explain: Insulin lowers blood sugar. If someone takes it and then does not eat, sugar can drop too low, causing shakiness, sweating and confusion. Fast sugar, such as fruit juice or glucose tablets, raises it within minutes. Food should only be given if the person is awake and can swallow, and an adult should get medical help.

scenario: A girl is diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. Her immune system has damaged the cells that make insulin. In which organ are these cells?
optionNotes: Has small clusters of insulin-making cells
explain: The pancreas has small clusters of cells, called islets, that make insulin. In type 1 diabetes, the immune system attacks these cells by mistake, so the body can no longer make enough insulin. People with type 1 diabetes need insulin every day for life. It is not caused by eating sweets.

scenario: A man feels tired and cold all the time and has gained weight without eating more. A blood test shows he has too little thyroxine. Which gland is not working hard enough?
explain: Thyroxine sets the speed at which cells burn energy. When the thyroid makes too little, everything slows down: the person feels tired and cold, and gains weight more easily. Doctors treat this with a daily tablet that replaces the missing hormone.

scenario: A woman eats well but keeps losing weight. She feels hot and shaky, and her heart races even at rest. A blood test shows one hormone level is far too high. Which one?
optionNotes: Too much speeds up the whole body
Too much would lower blood sugar
Affects sleep, not weight or heart
explain: Too much thyroxine is like pressing the body's accelerator all the time. Cells burn energy very fast, so the person loses weight, feels hot, sweats, shakes and has a fast heartbeat. This is called an overactive thyroid, and doctors can treat it with medicine.

scenario: A 12-year-old watches videos in bed until midnight and cannot fall asleep. The bright screen delays a hormone that makes us sleepy when it gets dark. Which hormone?
optionNotes: Released by the pineal gland in darkness
explain: The pineal gland in the brain releases melatonin when it gets dark, which tells the body it is time to sleep. Bright light, especially from screens, delays melatonin, so it is harder to fall asleep. Switching screens off an hour before bed helps the body's natural sleep signal.

scenario: An 11-year-old girl has had her first period and asks her doctor what is happening. The doctor explains that about once a month an egg is released. Which organ releases it?
explain: A girl has two ovaries, one on each side of the uterus. After puberty starts, about once a month one of them releases an egg, which travels down the oviduct. If the egg is not fertilised, the lining of the uterus is shed as a period. Starting periods is a normal part of growing up.

scenario: A student asks a doctor what forms right after a sperm and an egg fuse. It is a single cell that will divide again and again to become a baby. What is it called?
optionNotes: The single cell formed at fertilisation
Ball of cells formed after many divisions
Later stage, when body parts are visible
explain: When a sperm and an egg fuse, they form one cell called a zygote. The zygote divides again and again to form an embryo, a growing ball of cells that settles in the uterus. Once the main body parts can be seen, the developing baby is called a foetus.

scenario: Twin girls look exactly alike and have the same genes. The doctor says they are identical twins. How did they form?
options: Two eggs each fertilised by a different sperm
One egg fertilised by two sperm
optionNotes: Each half grows into a baby
One sperm can fertilise only one egg
explain: Identical twins form when one fertilised egg, the zygote, splits into two early on. Each part grows into a baby, so both have the same genes. Non-identical twins come from two separate eggs fertilised by two separate sperm, so they can look as different as ordinary brothers and sisters.

scenario: Arjun is 12. Most of his friends have suddenly grown taller and their voices are deeper, but his have not changed yet. He is healthy. What should the doctor tell him?
options: He needs growth injections right away
Puberty starts at different ages, and his may just come later
answer: Puberty starts at different ages, and his may just come later
optionNotes: Normal range is wide, roughly 9 to 14 in boys
Extra food does not start puberty
Not true; his bones are still growing
explain: Puberty is set off by hormones, and the timing differs from person to person. In boys it usually starts between about 9 and 14, so at 12 it is normal to be early or late. Late starters usually catch up. A doctor checks further only if there are no signs of puberty by around 14.

scenario: A student asks how a hormone made in a gland in the neck reaches cells in the toes, with no tube joining them. How does it travel?
options: Through the air in the lungs
optionNotes: Urine carries waste out of the body
Blood reaches every part of the body
explain: Endocrine glands have no ducts. They release hormones straight into the blood, which flows to every part of the body within about a minute. Only cells with the right receivers respond, the way only one lock opens for a key. That is why hormones can act far from where they were made.

notes: Tiny air sacs at the end
reason: The food pipe carries food; the other four are on the path air takes.
explain: Air travels a set path: in through the nose, down the windpipe, into two bronchi, through smaller and smaller tubes, and finally into tiny air sacs called alveoli. The food pipe sits right behind the windpipe in your neck, but it carries food and drink to the stomach, so it is part of digestion.

notes: Sugar from food, carried in blood
A tiny part of the air
reason: Glucose is a sugar from food; the other four are found in the air you breathe.
explain: The air you breathe is a mix of gases. Most of it is nitrogen, about a fifth is oxygen, and there is a little water vapour and a very small amount of carbon dioxide. Your body only takes in the oxygen. Glucose is a sugar that reaches your blood from digested food, not from the air.

notes: Upper-arm muscle that bends the elbow
Moves down to pull air in
Move up and out as you breathe in
Fill up and empty with each breath
Lift the ribs when you breathe in
reason: The biceps moves the arm; the other four move every time you breathe.
explain: Lungs have no muscles of their own, so other parts do the work. The diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs, pulls down, and the muscles between the ribs lift the rib cage up and out. The chest gets bigger and air flows into the lungs. Your biceps is in your upper arm and plays no part in breathing.

notes: Tiny bugs living in house dust
reason: Drinking water does not set off asthma; the other four can.
explain: In asthma, the airways are extra sensitive. Certain things, called triggers, make them swell, tighten and fill with mucus, so breathing becomes hard. Common triggers are dust mites, pollen, smoke and cold air. Knowing your triggers and avoiding them is a big part of keeping asthma under control.

reason: Fins are for swimming; the other four are ways animals take in oxygen.
explain: Every animal needs oxygen, but they collect it in different ways. Fish use gills to take oxygen dissolved in water. Insects have tiny holes called spiracles leading to air tubes. Earthworms absorb oxygen through their moist skin, and we use lungs. Fins help a fish swim and balance but do not take in any oxygen.

notes: Tiny hairs that sweep mucus up
Blasts out things stuck in airways
Diaphragm twitch with no cleaning job
reason: Hiccups do not protect the airways; the other four do.
explain: Your airways have a cleaning system. Nose hairs catch bigger bits of dust, sticky mucus traps smaller particles and germs, and tiny hairs called cilia sweep that mucus up to the throat to be swallowed. If something gets further in, a cough blasts it out. Hiccups are sudden twitches of the diaphragm and do not clean anything.

notes: Sticky brown gunk that coats lungs
Addictive chemical that keeps people smoking
Nutrient in fruits; not in smoke
Gas that blocks oxygen in blood
Harsh chemical also used in cleaners
reason: Vitamin C is a nutrient; the other four are harmful substances in cigarette smoke.
explain: Cigarette smoke contains thousands of chemicals. Tar coats the airways and damages the cilia, nicotine makes smoking addictive, and carbon monoxide takes up space in the blood that oxygen should use. Ammonia is one of many irritating chemicals. Vitamin C is a healthy nutrient found in fruits like amla and oranges; smoking actually lowers its level in the body.

reason: The diaphragm moving up happens when you breathe out; the other four happen when you breathe in.
explain: When you breathe in, the diaphragm tightens and flattens downwards and the ribs lift up and out. This makes the chest bigger, so air rushes in to fill the extra space. When you breathe out, the diaphragm relaxes and domes back up, the chest gets smaller, and air is pushed out.

notes: Infection that fills air sacs with fluid
Virus infection of the nose and throat
Yellow skin from a liver problem
Bacterial infection that mainly attacks lungs
reason: Jaundice is a liver problem; the other four affect the breathing system.
explain: Illnesses are often grouped by the part of the body they mainly affect. A cold affects the nose and throat, bronchitis the bronchi, pneumonia the air sacs, and tuberculosis mostly the lungs. Jaundice turns the skin and eyes yellow because the liver is not clearing a yellow substance from the blood, so it belongs to a different system.

notes: More room for gases to swap
Blood is right next to the air
reason: Thick muscle walls would block gas exchange; the other four help it.
explain: The alveoli are built for swapping gases. Their walls are only one cell thick and kept moist, so oxygen can dissolve and pass through quickly. Hundreds of millions of them give a huge surface area, and each is wrapped in capillaries so blood is right next to the air. A thick wall would make the journey too long.

notes: Released from food for cells to use
reason: Oxygen is used up by respiration in cells; the other four are produced by it.
explain: Breathing and respiration are different. Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration happens inside every cell: glucose combines with oxygen to release energy. This process also makes carbon dioxide, water and heat. So oxygen goes in, and the rest come out.

notes: Two main tubes inside the chest
Voice box, up in the neck
Air sacs deep inside the lungs
Small branching tubes inside the lungs
reason: The larynx sits in the neck; the other four are inside the chest.
explain: The breathing system has an upper part in the head and neck (nose, throat and larynx) and a lower part in the chest. Inside the chest, the windpipe splits into two bronchi, which branch into bronchioles ending in alveoli. Each lung is wrapped in a thin, slippery layer called the pleura. The larynx, or voice box, sits at the top of the windpipe in your neck.

items: Wearing a mask in heavy smog
notes: Stops cold and flu germs spreading
Fills the air with harmful smoke
reason: Burning garbage harms the lungs; the other four help protect them.
explain: Lungs stay healthy when they get clean air and are not exposed to germs and smoke. Exercise strengthens the breathing muscles, washing hands stops many chest infections spreading, and masks filter some pollution. Burning garbage releases smoke and harmful gases that irritate the airways, especially in people with asthma.

notes: Air from lungs passes the vocal cords
Controlled air through the vocal cords
Sudden blast of air from the lungs
Pushes air out of the lungs
reason: Blinking does not use air from the lungs; the other four do.
explain: Your lungs do more than bring in oxygen. The air you breathe out is used to talk, sing, cough and blow. When air passes the vocal cords in your voice box, they vibrate and make sound. Blinking is done by small muscles in your eyelids and uses no air at all.

notes: Measures how much air you blow out
Measures how fast you can blow out
Turns medicine into a mist to breathe in
reason: A blood pressure cuff checks the circulation; the other four test or treat the airways.
explain: A lung doctor uses tools to test and treat breathing. A spirometer and a peak flow meter measure how much air you can blow out and how fast, which shows whether the airways are narrow. Inhalers and nebulisers deliver medicine straight to the airways. A blood pressure cuff checks the heart and arteries instead.

notes: Holds its breath on dives, then surfaces
Takes oxygen from water with gills
Breathes air; dives to catch fish
reason: A shark uses gills; the other four sea animals breathe air with lungs.
explain: Living in the sea does not mean breathing water. Whales, dolphins, seals and sea lions are mammals, like us. They have lungs and must come to the surface to breathe air, even though they can hold their breath for a long time. A shark is a fish. Its gills take oxygen dissolved in water, so it never needs to come up for air.

notes: Blood vessels in the nose heat it
Happens in the alveoli, not the nose
Nose hairs and mucus catch it
Smell sensors high inside the nose
reason: Swapping oxygen into blood happens in the lungs; the nose does the other four.
explain: Your nose prepares air before it reaches your lungs. Blood vessels in its lining warm the air, the damp surface moistens it, and hairs and mucus trap dust. Smell sensors at the top also check what you are breathing. The actual swap of oxygen into the blood happens much deeper, in the alveoli. This is why breathing through your nose is better for your lungs than breathing through your mouth.

clues: The right one has three sections and the left one has only two, to make room for a neighbour.
Smoking turns these pink, spongy organs grey and damaged.
You have two of them, and they fill up like balloons each time you inhale.
explain: Your lungs are two spongy organs inside your rib cage. They take in oxygen from the air and get rid of carbon dioxide from the blood. The left lung is a little smaller than the right because the heart sits on that side.

clues: It separates the chest from the belly like a floor.
When it tightens and flattens, the chest gets bigger and air rushes in.
It is the large sheet under your lungs that does most of the work when you inhale.
explain: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle under your lungs. When it contracts, it flattens and pulls downwards, making space in the chest so air flows in. When it relaxes, it moves back up and pushes air out. It works on its own while you sleep, but you can also control it, for example when you hold your breath.

clues: There are hundreds of millions of them, giving a huge surface for swapping gases.
Each one is wrapped in a net of capillaries and has walls only one cell thick.
They are the bubble-shaped pockets at the very ends of your breathing tubes.
explain: Alveoli are tiny, balloon-like air sacs at the ends of the smallest airways. Oxygen passes through their thin walls into the blood in surrounding capillaries, and carbon dioxide passes the other way. Having so many of them gives the lungs a very large surface for this swap.

clues: Rings of cartilage shaped like the letter C stop it from collapsing.
At its bottom end it splits into two branches, one going to each lung.
It is the tube in front of your food pipe that carries what you inhale down to your chest.
explain: The windpipe, or trachea, is the tube that carries air from your throat down into your chest. C-shaped rings of cartilage hold it open, like the ridges of a vacuum-cleaner hose. You can feel these ridges if you gently touch the front of your neck.

clues: A small object breathed in by mistake most often gets stuck in the right one, which is wider and steeper.
Like the windpipe, they are held open by rings of cartilage.
They are the two passages that split off from the bottom of the windpipe, one into each side of the chest.
explain: At the bottom of the windpipe, the airway splits into two bronchi, one for each lung. Inside the lungs they keep dividing into thinner tubes called bronchioles, like the branches of an upside-down tree. When the bronchi become swollen and full of mucus, the illness is called bronchitis.

clues: It often runs in families and often begins in childhood.
Dust, pollen, smoke or cold air can make the airways tighten and swell.
During a flare-up the chest feels tight and a whistling sound comes when air goes out; a puffer helps.
explain: Asthma is a long-term condition in which the airways are extra sensitive. When something irritates them, the muscles around the airways tighten, the lining swells and makes extra mucus, so air struggles to get through. Reliever inhalers relax those muscles quickly, and daily preventer medicine prescribed by a doctor keeps the swelling down.
fact: Many famous athletes have asthma and compete at the highest level.

clues: It is a reflex: your body does it without you deciding to.
It blasts air up from your chest to clear food, dust or phlegm from your windpipe.
You should do it into your elbow so germs do not spread.
explain: A cough is a protective reflex. When something irritates your airways, you take a quick breath, close the top of your windpipe, build up pressure, and then release it in a burst. The rush of air carries the irritant out. A cough that lasts more than a few weeks should be checked by a doctor.

clues: Bright sunlight makes some people do this, and scientists are still not sure why.
Pepper, dust or pollen tickling the inside of your nostrils can set it off.
It is a sudden burst of air out through the nostrils and mouth, and your eyes usually shut.
explain: A sneeze is a reflex that clears the inside of your nose. When something irritates the lining, nerves send a message to the brain, which makes the chest and throat muscles push air out in a sudden blast. Sneezing into a tissue or your elbow stops germs from spreading to others.

clues: Tiny hairs called cilia sweep it up towards your throat, where you swallow it.
It traps dust, pollen and germs before they reach your lungs.
When you have a cold, extra amounts run out and you need a hanky.
explain: Mucus is a thick, wet layer that lines your nose and airways. It catches dust and germs so they do not reach the delicate alveoli. Your airways make some every day, and you swallow most of it without noticing. When you have a cold, your body makes much more to wash the germs out.

clues: Fire needs it to keep burning.
Your cells use it with food to release energy.
Green leaves give it off in sunlight, and you take it in every time you inhale.
explain: Oxygen is the gas your cells need to release energy from food. Your lungs take it from the air, and red blood cells carry it around the body. Plants release oxygen when they make food from sunlight, which is why forests and trees matter for the air we breathe.

clues: It makes the bubbles in fizzy drinks.
Your cells make it as waste when they release energy from food.
Your blood carries it to your lungs so you can get rid of it when you puff out.
explain: Carbon dioxide is a waste gas made by every cell during respiration. Blood carries it to the lungs, where it passes into the alveoli and is breathed out. Your brain watches its level closely: when it rises, as during exercise, the brain makes you breathe faster and deeper.

clues: Using it with a plastic spacer tube helps more of what is inside reach the airways.
Doctors teach children to shake it and then hold their breath for a few seconds after using it.
A person with tight, wheezy airways presses this small handheld device and sucks in a fine mist.
explain: An inhaler is a small device that sends a measured dose of medicine as a fine mist straight into the airways. Because the medicine goes right where it is needed, a small dose works quickly. Reliever inhalers open tight airways within minutes, while preventer inhalers are used daily to calm swelling. A doctor decides which one a person needs.

clues: Smoking slows them down and can destroy them.
They line your windpipe and wave back and forth many times a second.
They move like grass in the wind, pushing dirty phlegm up to your throat.
explain: Cilia are microscopic hair-like parts on the cells lining your airways. They beat together in waves, moving a layer of mucus and trapped dirt up towards the throat, like a slow conveyor belt. Smoking damages cilia, so dirt stays in the lungs, and smokers have to cough more to clear it.

clues: It is made of bendy cartilage and sits just behind the base of your tongue.
It folds down over your voice box like a lid every time you eat.
If you laugh while drinking, it may not shut in time, and you start coughing.
explain: Your throat is shared by air and food, so the body needs a traffic controller. The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped flap that tips down over the entrance to the windpipe when you swallow, sending food into the food pipe instead. If something slips past, a cough pushes it back out.

clues: It makes a bump at the front of the neck that is bigger in grown men, sometimes called the Adam's apple.
Two folds inside it vibrate when air from your lungs passes through them.
If you shout too much at a match, it gets sore and you go hoarse.
explain: The voice box, or larynx, sits at the top of the windpipe. Inside it are two vocal cords. When you talk, they come together and vibrate as air from your lungs passes between them. Tighter cords make a higher note. During puberty, the voice box of boys grows larger, which makes their voices deeper.

clues: Eating too fast or gulping fizzy drinks can bring them on.
A sheet of muscle under your lungs suddenly jerks, and your vocal cords snap shut.
These little squeaky noises keep coming every few seconds and usually stop by themselves.
explain: Hiccups happen when the diaphragm suddenly tightens by itself. Air rushes in, and a split second later the vocal cords snap shut, making the familiar sound. They are harmless and usually stop within a few minutes. Scientists are still not certain what purpose, if any, they serve.

clues: Tadpoles have them, but most adult frogs lose them.
They are feathery, red and full of blood vessels to soak up dissolved oxygen.
A shark or a tuna uses these slits on the sides of its head to get oxygen.
explain: Gills do the same job as lungs, but for animals that live in water. Water flows in through the mouth and out over the gills. Their thin, feathery folds are packed with blood vessels, so oxygen dissolved in the water passes into the blood. Human lungs cannot do this, which is why we cannot breathe underwater.

scenario: During a football game, a girl with asthma starts coughing and wheezing and says her chest feels tight. She has her reliever inhaler with her. What should be done first while an adult is called?
options: Make her keep running to push through it
Help her sit upright and use her reliever inhaler
Give her a cold fizzy drink
Lay her flat on the ground
answer: Help her sit upright and use her reliever inhaler
optionNotes: Exercise can make the flare-up worse
explain: In an asthma flare-up, the muscles around the airways tighten. A reliever inhaler relaxes those muscles and opens the airways within minutes. Sitting upright and staying calm make breathing easier. If she does not improve quickly, or gets worse, an adult should call for emergency help.

scenario: At lunch, a boy suddenly starts choking on food. He is red in the face but can still cough loudly and speak. What should you do first?
options: Give him a glass of water
Encourage him to keep coughing and call an adult
Reach into his mouth with your fingers to grab it
answer: Encourage him to keep coughing and call an adult
optionNotes: A strong cough is the best way to clear it
explain: If someone can cough and speak, air is still getting through, and a strong cough is the body's best way to push the food out. Stay with him and get an adult. If he cannot cough, speak or breathe, a trained adult gives back blows and abdominal thrusts and calls emergency services.

scenario: Ravi, 9, often wheezes and coughs at night. It gets worse with dust and when he runs, and his mother has the same problem. He has no fever. What is the most likely condition?
optionNotes: Infection that usually brings high fever
Long infection with fever and weight loss
Runny nose; clears up in about a week
Triggered wheeze that runs in families
explain: Wheezing that keeps coming back, gets worse with triggers like dust and exercise, and is often worse at night points to asthma. It often runs in families. The lack of fever suggests no infection. A pulmonologist can confirm it with a breathing test and give medicines to control it.

scenario: A doctor asks a patient to take a deep breath and blow out as hard and fast as possible into a tube attached to a machine. The machine measures how much air comes out and how quickly. What is the machine?
optionNotes: Used to listen to chest sounds
Clip that measures oxygen in blood
Measures air blown out and its speed
explain: A spirometer measures how much air your lungs can hold and how fast you can blow it out. If the airways are narrow, as in asthma, air comes out more slowly than expected. Doctors use the test to diagnose lung conditions and to check whether treatment is working.

scenario: A nurse clips a small device onto a patient's fingertip. It shines light through the finger and shows a number like 98%. What does that number tell the doctor?
options: How much oxygen the blood is carrying
answer: How much oxygen the blood is carrying
optionNotes: Needs a drop of blood to test
explain: This device is a pulse oximeter. Haemoglobin carrying oxygen absorbs light differently from haemoglobin without it, so the device can tell how full of oxygen the blood is. In a healthy person the reading is usually 95% or higher. A low number tells doctors the lungs may not be taking in enough oxygen.

scenario: A man has had a high fever and a bad cough for five days. The doctor hears crackling sounds in his chest and wants a picture of the inside of his lungs. Which test is best?
optionNotes: Makes a picture of the lungs
Checks kidneys and urine, not lungs
Measures breath but makes no picture
explain: X-rays pass easily through air but are blocked by bone and fluid. On a chest X-ray, healthy lungs look dark because they are full of air. An infected area filled with fluid shows up as a white patch, which helps the doctor see where the problem is.

scenario: A chest X-ray shows that many air sacs in part of a patient's lung are filled with fluid and pus because of an infection. Oxygen cannot pass into the blood there. What is this illness?
optionNotes: Narrowed airways, not fluid-filled air sacs
Infection that fills the air sacs
Swollen bronchi, not the air sacs
explain: Pneumonia is an infection deep in the lungs, in the alveoli where gas exchange happens. The sacs fill with fluid and pus, so oxygen cannot reach the blood in that area. People get fever, cough and fast breathing. Bacteria, viruses or fungi can cause it, and doctors choose treatment based on the cause.

scenario: A man has smoked for 20 years. He coughs every morning and gets breathless walking uphill. What is the most helpful step he can take for his lungs?
optionNotes: Stops further damage; some healing follows
Stale air does not help the lungs
explain: Smoke damages the cilia and slowly breaks down the walls of the alveoli, so less oxygen gets in. Stopping smoking prevents further damage. Over the following months the cilia recover and coughing often eases. Stopping helps at any age, and doctors can give support to make it easier.

scenario: A family drives from Delhi to Leh in Ladakh, over 3,000 metres high. On the first day everyone feels breathless while walking. Why?
options: There is no oxygen up there
Thinner air gives less oxygen per breath
The air has extra carbon dioxide
answer: Thinner air gives less oxygen per breath
optionNotes: Oxygen is still about one-fifth of the air
Lower air pressure means fewer oxygen molecules per breath
Lungs do not shrink in the cold
Carbon dioxide levels are not higher there
explain: High up, the air is still about one-fifth oxygen, but the air pressure is lower, so each breath holds fewer oxygen molecules. The body responds by breathing faster. Over a few days it adjusts, which is why travellers to high places are told to rest on the first day and go up slowly.

scenario: A boy gulped a fizzy drink and now makes a 'hic' sound every few seconds. Which muscle is suddenly twitching?
optionNotes: Moves food and helps you talk
explain: Hiccups are sudden twitches of the diaphragm, the dome-shaped breathing muscle under your lungs. Each twitch pulls in a quick gulp of air, and the vocal cords snap shut, making the 'hic'. A stretched stomach from gulping food or fizzy drinks can set it off. Hiccups usually stop on their own.

scenario: A girl has a runny nose, sneezing and a mild sore throat for three days, with only a slight temperature. The doctor says a virus caused it. What is the best advice?
options: Rest, drink fluids and wash hands often
answer: Rest, drink fluids and wash hands often
optionNotes: Antibiotics do not work on viruses
Tires the body while it fights the virus
The body needs food to recover
explain: A common cold is caused by a virus that infects the nose and throat. Antibiotics only kill bacteria, so they do not help. The body clears a cold by itself in about a week, and rest and fluids support it. Washing hands stops the virus from spreading. See a doctor if breathing becomes hard or a high fever develops.

scenario: The air quality in a city is 'severe' because of smoke and dust. A boy with asthma wants to play cricket outside for two hours. What is the best advice for today?
options: Stay indoors and play a quieter game today
Play outside; it will make his lungs stronger
Play outside but breathe only through the mouth
